items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency’s Small Business/Self- Employed Division, Specialty Collection– Insolvency Office in Houston, Texas. On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment on the bases of disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity) when: 1. 1.Beginning February 2021 to the present, she has been denied paid leave under the Family Medical and Leave Act (FMLA); 2. On June 19, 2021, a manager reassigned all of a retired co-worker’s complex cases to her; 3. On August 3, 2021, she was denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave; 4. On August 24, 2021, her final appeal of a requested reasonable accommodation was denied; and 5. On October 26, 2021, her supervisor denied her official time request to work on her EEO complaint. Claims 1 & 3 – Leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Complainant challenged leave issues, including her receipt of Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges and placement in Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status in a prior EEO complaint before an EEOC Administrative Judge. On May 25, 2022, the Administrative Judge in that case found that the Agency had proven that it had placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021, because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work. In the instant complaint, Complainant again raised leave issues previously adjudicated, including her February and March 2021 receipt of AWOL charges and placement in LWOP status. Complainant also alleges that on August 3, 2021, her manager denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave. Complainant’s first-line supervisor (Supervisor1) explained that management’s calculations showed that Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. Specifically, the Agency’s February 26, 2021, letter to Complainant regarding her request for FMLA provided that Complainant had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. As such, on March 1, 2021, and on other dates, Supervisor notified Complainant that she had no paid leave available to use under FMLA. On various dates, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor granted Complainant FMLA-LWOP, rather than paid leave. Complainant did not request an audit of her leave until August 5, 2021. The audit of Complainant’s leave, conducted by a payroll representative, showed that Complainant had some paid leave available to use under FMLA. Accordingly, management retroactively granted Complainant paid leave, including for August 3, 2021. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave that she requested and was entitled to receive. Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding leave. Claim 2 – Reassignment of Casework In June 2021, one of Complainant’s GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired. Complainant claimed that Supervisor emailed Complainant (a GS- 12) and two other GS-12 employees in the group to inform them that the now- retired employee’s cases would be reassigned among the three GS-12s. Complainant asserted that she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave. 2 The Administrative Judge found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave, and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed]. Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. Supervisor also explained that all reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant’s grade level. Supervisor further explained that the work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists in the group, based upon the alphabetical order of case names. The documentary record also contains a spreadsheet, provided by Supervisor1, showing the case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists in the group. The record is devoid of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim. Claim 4 –Reasonable Accommodations On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested the following accommodations: (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her reasonable accommodation request to include reassignment. Complainant concedes that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. The Agency’s Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021, to hold an interactive meeting. Regarding her request for reduced workload and/or reassignment, the Agency issued a denial, noting that there was no medical explanation supporting Complainant’s need for such accommodations. The Agency’s denial also noted that lowering Complainant’s caseload would lower performance or production standards and would compromise the Agency’s ability to achieve its mission. Moreover, with an inventory of then only 25 cases, the undisputed record showed that Complainant already maintained a caseload well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held. 3 Regarding her request for reassignment, the Agency’s denial noted that Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (i.e., granted only when an employee is unable to meet the essential functions of her position). For example, to support a previous 2018 request for reduced inventory, Complainant’s psychologist had noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases. When Complainant requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency explained that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence showed that Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors, and not because of any medical impairment’s effect on her ability to perform the essential functions of her job. To accommodate Complainant’s physical limitations, in response to Complainant’s May 6, 2021 reasonable accommodation request, the Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so that she could print and mail letters to taxpayers. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later averred that she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper. The Agency denied Complainant’s request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the Agency’s denial of her reconsideration request. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations (Director) denied Complainant’s appeal. The denial noted that Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency’s offer to provide her with a smaller portable printer that she could lift. Further, the denial noted that Complainant had an already-reduced workload and was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing the essential functions of her job. Claim 5 – Official Time On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested to use official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to respond to an EEO Investigator’s request that Complainant complete an affidavit for the instant complaint. Complainant availed herself of six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021. Despite being provided these hours, Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021. On October 25, 2021, Supervisor approved Complainant’s request to use additional official time that day. On October 26, 2021, Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline to complete her affidavit. In response, OCRD noted that Complainant could request an extension from the investigator if she needed more time to complete the affidavit. After receiving OCRD’s response, Complainant asked Supervisor for official time to complete the affidavit that day. When Supervisor asked Complainant if she had completed the affidavit, Complainant told Supervisor that she had two questions remaining. Because Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time and because OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact the investigator if she needed an extension of her deadline, Supervisor denied Complainant’s request to continue working on her affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Further, the AJ found that there was no evidence demonstrating that the conduct at issue was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

## COMPLAINT FILING AND COMPLAINANT STATUS
On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint. At the time of the events giving rise to the complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency's Small Business/Self-Employed Division, Specialty Collection–Insolvency Office in Houston, Texas.

## BASES AND ALLEGATIONS
Complainant alleged discrimination and hostile work environment based on disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity). The complaint included five specific allegations:

1. **Beginning February 2021 to the present**: Denial of paid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)
2. **June 19, 2021**: Manager reassigned all complex cases of a retired co-worker to her
3. **August 3, 2021**: Denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave
4. **August 24, 2021**: Final appeal of requested reasonable accommodation was denied
5. **October 26, 2021**: Supervisor denied official time request to work on EEO complaint

## CLAIM 1 & 3 – FMLA LEAVE ISSUES

### Prior Administrative Adjudication
On May 25, 2022, an EEOC Administrative Judge found in a prior case that the Agency had proven it placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021 because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work.

### Factual Record
- **February 26, 2021**: Agency letter to Complainant regarding FMLA request stated Complainant had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021
- **March 1, 2021 and other dates**: Supervisor notified Complainant she had no paid leave available to use under FMLA
- **Various dates, including August 3, 2021**: Supervisor granted Complainant FMLA-LWOP rather than paid leave
- **August 5, 2021**: Complainant requested audit of leave
- Payroll representative audit showed Complainant had some paid leave available under FMLA
- Management retroactively granted Complainant paid leave, including for August 3, 2021

### Agency Response
Supervisor1 explained that management's calculations showed Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave that she requested and was entitled to receive. Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding leave.

## CLAIM 2 – REASSIGNMENT OF CASEWORK

### Factual Record
In June 2021, one of Complainant's GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired. Supervisor emailed Complainant (a GS-12) and two other GS-12 employees informing them the retired employee's cases would be reassigned among the three GS-12s. Complainant asserted she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave.

### Agency Response
Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. All reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant's grade level. The work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists based upon the alphabetical order of case names. Supervisor1 provided a spreadsheet showing case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists. The record contained no similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim.

### Pending Appeal
The Administrative Judge in a related case found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed].

## CLAIM 4 – REASONABLE ACCOMMODATIONS

### Initial Requests
- **May 6, 2021**: Complainant requested (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload
- **May 18, 2021**: Complainant amended request to include reassignment

### Agency Interactive Meeting and Denial
The Agency's Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021. The Agency issued a denial regarding reduced workload and/or reassignment, noting:
- No medical explanation supported Complainant's need for such accommodations
- Lowering Complainant's caseload would lower performance or production standards and compromise the Agency's ability to achieve its mission
- Complainant's inventory was then only 25 cases, well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held
- Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (granted only when an employee is unable to meet essential functions of her position)

### Supporting Evidence from Prior Requests
- **2018**: Complainant's psychologist noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases
- **March 2020**: When Complainant requested reassignment, the Agency explained she failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet essential functions. Evidence showed Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with supervisors, not because of any medical impairment's effect on ability to perform essential functions

### Approved Accommodation and Complainant's Response
The Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so she could print and mail letters. While awaiting delivery, Complainant's management agreed to send Complainant's correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for it and its paper. Complainant later averred she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper.

### Appeals Process and Final Denial
The Agency denied Complainant's request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed. **On August 24, 2021**, the **Director of Collection Operations** denied Complainant's appeal, noting that:
- Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency's offer to provide a smaller portable printer that she could lift
- Complainant had an already-reduced workload
- Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing essential functions of her job

### Complainant's Concession
During investigation, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties.

## CLAIM 5 – OFFICIAL TIME

### Factual Record
- **October 20, 2021**: Complainant requested official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. October 20 through 11:30 a.m. October 21 to respond to EEO Investigator's request to complete an affidavit
- Complainant used six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021
- Complainant did not complete affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021
- **October 25, 2021**: Supervisor approved Complainant's request for additional official time that day
- **October 26, 2021**: Complainant emailed Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request extension of deadline to complete affidavit. OCRD responded that Complainant could request extension from investigator if needed

### Supervisor's Decision
When Complainant asked Supervisor for official time on October 26, 2021, Supervisor asked if Complainant had completed the affidavit. Complainant stated she had two questions remaining. **Supervisor denied Complainant's request** to continue working on affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021, because:
- Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time
- OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact investigator if she needed deadline extension

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

On the date referenced in the record, an **EEOC Administrative Judge** issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. The AJ **applied the following criteria and analysis**:

### Hostile Work Environment Finding
The AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment and found no evidence demonstrating that the conduct was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

### Leave Claims (Claims 1 & 3)
- Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside protected classes were treated more favorably regarding FMLA or other leave entitlements

### Reassignment Claim (Claim 2)
- Record evidence showed reassigned cases from retired co-worker were split equally among Complainant and two Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level, and appropriateness given Complainant's low workload

### Reasonable Accommodation Claim (Claim 4)
Regarding Complainant's May 6, 2021 request, the AJ determined:
- Complainant requested manager/secretary assist printing and mailing letters and requested reduced workload
- Complainant amended request on May 18, 2021 to include reassignment
- During investigation, Complainant admitted her impairment did not limit ability to perform any essential job duties
- Complainant did not adduce probative evidence that previously offered accommodations (post of duty with telework away from manager and communication primarily by email) did not enable performance of essential functions

Regarding reduced inventory request:
- An agency is not required to change production standards or lower employee quota for cases
- Complainant provided no evidence she could not adequately perform assignments given she had unusually low inventory of only 25 cases

Regarding portable printer accommodation:
- After interactive meeting, Agency approved lightweight, portable printer
- While awaiting delivery, management agreed to send Complainant's correspondence
- Before delivery, Complainant requested cancellation stating she did not wish to be held accountable for printer and paper
- Management continued to print and mail letters
- Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of Rehabilitation Act

### Official Time Claim (Claim 5)
- Agency's grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete affidavit despite investigator's numerous questions
- Record showed Complainant's time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in prior complaints
- Agency was entitled to limit official time to 18 hours and have Complainant seek additional time from investigator

### Overall Conclusion
The AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or hostile work environment as alleged.

## FINAL AGENCY ACTION
The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

## COMPLAINT FILING AND COMPLAINANT STATUS
On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint. At the time of the events giving rise to the complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency's Small Business/Self-Employed Division, Specialty Collection–Insolvency Office in Houston, Texas.

## BASES AND ALLEGATIONS
Complainant alleged discrimination and hostile work environment based on disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity). The complaint included five specific allegations:

1. **Beginning February 2021 to the present**: Denial of paid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)
2. **June 20, 2021**: Manager reassigned all complex cases of a retired co-worker to her
3. **August 3, 2021**: Denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave
4. **August 24, 2021**: Final appeal of requested reasonable accommodation was denied
5. **October 26, 2021**: Supervisor denied official time request to work on EEO complaint

## CLAIM 1 & 3 – FMLA LEAVE ISSUES

### Prior Administrative Adjudication
On May 25, 2022, an EEOC Administrative Judge found in a prior case that the Agency had proven it placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021 because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work.

### Factual Record
- **February 26, 2021**: Agency letter to Complainant regarding FMLA request stated Complainant had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021
- **March 1, 2021 and other dates**: Supervisor notified Complainant she had no paid leave available to use under FMLA
- **Various dates, including August 3, 2021**: Supervisor granted Complainant FMLA-LWOP rather than paid leave
- **August 5, 2021**: Complainant requested audit of leave
- Payroll representative audit showed Complainant had some paid leave available under FMLA
- Management retroactively granted Complainant paid leave, including for August 3, 2021

### Agency Response
Supervisor1 explained that management's calculations showed Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave that she requested and was entitled to receive. Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding leave.

## CLAIM 2 – REASSIGNMENT OF CASEWORK

### Factual Record
In June 2021, one of Complainant's GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired. Supervisor emailed Complainant (a GS-12) and two other GS-12 employees informing them the retired employee's cases would be reassigned among the three GS-12s. Complainant asserted she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave.

### Agency Response
Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. All reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant's grade level. The work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists based upon the alphabetical order of case names. Supervisor1 provided a spreadsheet showing case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists. The record contained no similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim.

### Pending Appeal
The Administrative Judge in a related case found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed].

## CLAIM 4 – REASONABLE ACCOMMODATIONS

### Initial Requests
- **May 6, 2021**: Complainant requested (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload
- **May 18, 2021**: Complainant amended request to include reassignment

### Agency Interactive Meeting and Denial
The Agency's Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021. The Agency issued a denial regarding reduced workload and/or reassignment, noting:
- No medical explanation supported Complainant's need for such accommodations
- Lowering Complainant's caseload would lower performance or production standards and compromise the Agency's ability to achieve its mission
- Complainant's inventory was then only 25 cases, well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held
- Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (granted only when an employee is unable to meet essential functions of her position)

### Supporting Evidence from Prior Requests
- **2018**: Complainant's psychologist noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases
- **March 2020**: When Complainant requested reassignment, the Agency explained she failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet essential functions. Evidence showed Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with supervisors, not because of any medical impairment's effect on ability to perform essential functions

### Approved Accommodation and Complainant's Response
The Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so she could print and mail letters. While awaiting delivery, Complainant's management agreed to send Complainant's correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for it and its paper. Complainant later averred she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper.

### Appeals Process and Final Denial
The Agency denied Complainant's request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed. **On August 24, 2021**, the **Director of Collection Operations** denied Complainant's appeal, noting that:
- Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency's offer to provide a smaller portable printer that she could lift
- Complainant had an already-reduced workload
- Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing essential functions of her job

### Complainant's Concession
During investigation, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties.

## CLAIM 5 – OFFICIAL TIME

### Factual Record
- **October 20, 2021**: Complainant requested official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. October 20 through 11:30 a.m. October 21 to respond to EEO Investigator's request to complete an affidavit
- Complainant used six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021
- Complainant did not complete affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021
- **October 25, 2021**: Supervisor approved Complainant's request for additional official time that day
- **October 26, 2021**: Complainant emailed Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request extension of deadline to complete affidavit. OCRD responded that Complainant could request extension from investigator if needed

### Supervisor's Decision
When Complainant asked Supervisor for official time on October 26, 2021, Supervisor asked if Complainant had completed the affidavit. Complainant stated she had two questions remaining. **Supervisor denied Complainant's request** to continue working on affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021, because:
- Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time
- OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact investigator if she needed deadline extension

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

On the date referenced in the record, an **EEOC Administrative Judge** issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. The AJ **applied the following criteria and analysis**:

### Hostile Work Environment Finding
The AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment and found no evidence demonstrating that the conduct was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

### Leave Claims (Claims 1 & 3)
- Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside protected classes were treated more favorably regarding FMLA or other leave entitlements

### Reassignment Claim (Claim 2)
- Record evidence showed reassigned cases from retired co-worker were split equally among Complainant and two Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level, and appropriateness given Complainant's low workload

### Reasonable Accommodation Claim (Claim 4)
Regarding Complainant's May 6, 2021 request, the AJ determined:
- Complainant requested manager/secretary assist printing and mailing letters and requested reduced workload
- Complainant amended request on May 18, 2021 to include reassignment
- During investigation, Complainant admitted her impairment did not limit ability to perform any essential job duties
- Complainant did not adduce probative evidence that previously offered accommodations (post of duty with telework away from manager and communication primarily by email) did not enable performance of essential functions

Regarding reduced inventory request:
- An agency is not required to change production standards or lower employee quota for cases
- Complainant provided no evidence she could not adequately perform assignments given she had unusually low inventory of only 25 cases

Regarding portable printer accommodation:
- After interactive meeting, Agency approved lightweight, portable printer
- While awaiting delivery, management agreed to send Complainant's correspondence
- Before delivery, Complainant requested cancellation stating she did not wish to be held accountable for printer and paper
- Management continued to print and mail letters
- Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of Rehabilitation Act

### Official Time Claim (Claim 5)
- Agency's grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete affidavit despite investigator's numerous questions
- Record showed Complainant's time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in prior complaints
- Agency was entitled to limit official time to 18 hours and have Complainant seek additional time from investigator

### Overall Conclusion
The AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or hostile work environment as alleged.

## FINAL AGENCY ACTION
The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

Claim 4 –Reasonable Accommodations On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested the following accommodations: (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her reasonable accommodation request to include reassignment. Complainant concedes that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. The Agency’s Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021, to hold an interactive meeting. Regarding her request for reduced workload and/or reassignment, the Agency issued a denial, noting that there was no medical explanation supporting Complainant’s need for such accommodations. The Agency’s denial also noted that lowering Complainant’s caseload would lower performance or production standards and would compromise the Agency’s ability to achieve its mission. Moreover, with an inventory of then only 25 cases, the undisputed record showed that Complainant already maintained a caseload well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held. 3 Regarding her request for reassignment, the Agency’s denial noted that Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (i.e., granted only when an employee is unable to meet the essential functions of her position). For example, to support a previous 2018 request for reduced inventory, Complainant’s psychologist had noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases. When Complainant requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency explained that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later averred that she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations (Director) denied Complainant’s appeal. The denial noted that Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency’s offer to provide her with a smaller portable printer that she could lift. Further, the denial noted that Complainant had an already-reduced workload and was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing the essential functions of her job. Claim 5 – Official Time On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested to use official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to respond to an EEO Investigator’s request that Complainant complete an affidavit for the instant complaint. Complainant availed herself of six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021. Despite being provided these hours, Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021. On October 25, 2021, Supervisor approved Complainant’s request to use additional official time that day. On October 26, 2021, Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline to complete her affidavit. In response, OCRD noted that Complainant could request an extension from the investigator if she needed more time to complete the affidavit. After receiving OCRD’s response, Complainant asked Supervisor for official time to complete the affidavit that day. When Supervisor asked Complainant if she had completed the affidavit, Complainant told Supervisor that she had two questions remaining. Because Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time and because OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact the investigator if she needed an extension of her deadline, Supervisor denied Complainant’s request to continue working on her affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Further, the AJ found that there was no evidence demonstrating that the conduct at issue was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# Case File Summary

## Citation note
The record provided contains no ROI page numbers, exhibit numbers, or other record citations, and none are supplied here. The only record reference is the spreadsheet of case assignments that Supervisor1 provided (Claim 2). The EEOC docket number for the pending appeal was removed from the record. The record also gives no date for the AJ's summary judgment decision or the Agency's final order.

## Parties and procedural posture
- **Complainant:** GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist, Small Business/Self-Employed Division, Specialty Collection–Insolvency Office, Houston, Texas.
- **Complaint:** Filed September 17, 2021. It alleged discrimination and a hostile work environment based on disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity).
- **Claims:**
  1. Denial of paid FMLA leave from February 2021 to the present.
  2. Reassignment of a retired co-worker's complex cases to her on June 19, 2021.
  3. Denial of eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave on August 3, 2021.
  4. Denial of her final appeal of a reasonable accommodation request on August 24, 2021.
  5. Denial of her official time request on October 26, 2021.
- **Procedure:** After the investigation, the Agency gave Complainant the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing. She timely requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ.
- **Decision-maker:** The AJ issued a summary judgment decision for the Agency. The Agency then issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding that Complainant did not prove discrimination.

## Claims 1 and 3: FMLA leave
- **Prior decision:** In a prior EEO complaint, an EEOC AJ found on May 25, 2022 that the Agency had proven it placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021. Complainant had depleted her paid leave balances and failed to report to work. She raised the same February and March 2021 issues again in this complaint.
- **Supervisor1's account:**
  - Management's calculations showed Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021.
  - The Agency's February 26, 2021 FMLA letter said she had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021 and December 3, 2021.
  - On March 1, 2021 and other dates, Supervisor notified her she had no paid FMLA leave available. On various dates, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor granted FMLA-LWOP instead.
- **Audit:**
  - Complainant did not request an audit until August 5, 2021.
  - The audit, done by a payroll representative, showed she had some paid leave available.
  - Management then retroactively granted paid leave, including for August 3, 2021.
- **Complainant's statement:** She conceded she ultimately received all the paid leave she requested and was entitled to.
- **Comparators:** She identified no similarly situated employees treated more favorably.

## Claim 2: Reassignment of casework
- **Facts:** A GS-12 co-worker retired in June 2021. According to Complainant, Supervisor emailed her and two other GS-12 employees that the retired employee's cases would be split among the three.
- **Complainant's position:** She should not have received the cases because she had a pending reasonable accommodation request and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave.
- **Prior AJ finding:** An AJ found she was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency met all its Rehabilitation Act obligations. That appeal is pending (docket number removed). The record does not clearly say this was the prior case.
- **Supervisor's explanation:**
  - Assigning inventory was her job.
  - All the work was appropriate for Complainant's grade level.
  - The work was split among the three GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists by the alphabetical order of case names.
- **Documentary evidence:** The spreadsheet from Supervisor1 shows the case assignments.
- **Comparators:** The record contains no similarly situated employees treated more favorably.

## Claim 4: Reasonable accommodation
- **Requests:**
  - May 6, 2021: Complainant asked that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters, and for a reduced workload.
  - May 18, 2021: She amended the request to add reassignment.
  - She conceded her impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties.
- **Interactive meeting:** The Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with her on May 21, 2021.
- **Denial of reduced workload and reassignment (the Agency's reasons):**
  - There was no medical explanation supporting the need.
  - Lowering her caseload would lower performance or production standards and compromise the mission.
  - Her inventory was only 25 cases, well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below her typical caseload.
  - Reassignment is the accommodation of last resort, granted only when an employee cannot meet the essential functions of her position.
  - In a previous 2018 request, her psychologist had noted she desired roughly 38–40 cases.
  - When she requested reassignment in March 2020, she submitted no medical documentation showing she could not perform the essential functions. The evidence showed she wanted reassignment because of an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors.
- **Printer accommodation:**
  - The Agency approved a small portable printer, and management agreed to send her correspondence in the meantime.
  - Before delivery, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. She later averred she could not lift either the printer or its paper.
- **Appeal:**
  - The Agency denied her request for reconsideration.
  - She appealed on July 12, 2021.
  - On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations denied the appeal.
  - The Director's denial noted that she had summarily rejected the offered printer, already had a reduced workload, and was not eligible for reassignment because she could perform the essential functions of her job.

## Claim 5: Official time
- **Request:** On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested official time from about 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to complete an affidavit requested by the EEO Investigator.
- **Time used:** She used six hours on October 20 and four hours on October 21. She had not finished the affidavit and asked for more time on October 25.
- **October 25:** Supervisor approved additional official time that day.
- **October 26:**
  - Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension. OCRD responded that she could request an extension from the investigator.
  - She then asked Supervisor for more official time that day and said she had two questions remaining.
  - Supervisor denied the request. The stated reasons were that she had already received approximately 18 hours and that OCRD had told her to contact the investigator for an extension.

## AJ's summary judgment findings (decision-maker: AJ)
- **Hostile work environment:** The incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive.
- **Animus:** There was no evidence the conduct was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. Complainant did not show that similarly situated employees outside her protected classes were treated more favorably on FMLA or other leave.
- **Casework:** The reassigned cases were split equally among three Bankruptcy Specialists for unrebutted reasons of grade, skill level, and suitability given Complainant's low workload.
- **Accommodation:**
  - Complainant admitted her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties.
  - She offered no probative evidence that previously offered accommodations (a post of duty with telework away from her manager, and communication primarily by email) failed to let her perform the essential functions.
  - The record supported denying reduced inventory, because an agency need not change production standards such as lowering a case quota. She had an unusually low inventory of 25 cases and no evidence she could not perform her assignments.
  - After the interactive meeting, the Agency approved a lightweight portable printer. Management sent her correspondence meanwhile and continued to print and mail her letters after she cancelled the printer.
  - The AJ concluded the Agency did not deny reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act.
- **Official time:** The 18 hours granted was objectively reasonable to complete the affidavit despite the investigators' numerous questions. Her time was spent including information and documentation she had provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit official time to 18 hours and to have her seek more from the investigator.
- **Conclusion:** Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged.

## Outcome
The Agency issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding that Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged.

Complainant asserted that she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave. 2 The Administrative Judge found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave, and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed]. Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. Supervisor also explained that all reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant’s grade level. Supervisor further explained that the work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists in the group, based upon the alphabetical order of case names. The documentary record also contains a spreadsheet, provided by Supervisor1, showing the case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists in the group. The record is devoid of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim. Claim 4 –Reasonable Accommodations On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested the following accommodations: (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her reasonable accommodation request to include reassignment. Complainant concedes that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. The Agency’s Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021, to hold an interactive meeting. Regarding her request for reduced workload and/or reassignment, the Agency issued a denial, noting that there was no medical explanation supporting Complainant’s need for such accommodations. The Agency’s denial also noted that lowering Complainant’s caseload would lower performance or production standards and would compromise the Agency’s ability to achieve its mission. Moreover, with an inventory of then only 25 cases, the undisputed record showed that Complainant already maintained a caseload well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held. 3 Regarding her request for reassignment, the Agency’s denial noted that Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (i.e., granted only when an employee is unable to meet the essential functions of her position). For example, to support a previous 2018 request for reduced inventory, Complainant’s psychologist had noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases. When Complainant requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency explained that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence showed that Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors, and not because of any medical impairment’s effect on her ability to perform the essential functions of her job. To accommodate Complainant’s physical limitations, in response to Complainant’s May 6, 2021 reasonable accommodation request, the Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so that she could print and mail letters to taxpayers. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later averred that she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper. The Agency denied Complainant’s request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the Agency’s denial of her reconsideration request. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations (Director) denied Complainant’s appeal. The denial noted that Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency’s offer to provide her with a smaller portable printer that she could lift. Further, the denial noted that Complainant had an already-reduced workload and was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing the essential functions of her job. Claim 5 – Official Time On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested to use official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to respond to an EEO Investigator’s request that Complainant complete an affidavit for the instant complaint. Complainant availed herself of six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021. Despite being provided these hours, Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021. On October 25, 2021, Supervisor approved Complainant’s request to use additional official time that day. On October 26, 2021, Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline to complete her affidavit. In response, OCRD noted that Complainant could request an extension from the investigator if she needed more time to complete the affidavit. After receiving OCRD’s response, Complainant asked Supervisor for official time to complete the affidavit that day. When Supervisor asked Complainant if she had completed the affidavit, Complainant told Supervisor that she had two questions remaining. Because Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time and because OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact the investigator if she needed an extension of her deadline, Supervisor denied Complainant’s request to continue working on her affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Further, the AJ found that there was no evidence demonstrating that the conduct at issue was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# Case File Summary

## Citation note
The record provided contains no ROI page numbers, exhibit numbers, or other record citations, and none are supplied here. The only record reference is the spreadsheet of case assignments that Supervisor1 provided (Claim 2). The EEOC docket number for the pending appeal was not removed from the record. The record also gives no date for the AJ's summary judgment decision or the Agency's final order.

## Parties and procedural posture
- **Complainant:** GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist, Small Business/Self-Employed Division, Specialty Collection–Insolvency Office, Houston, Texas.
- **Complaint:** Filed September 17, 2021. It alleged discrimination and a hostile work environment based on disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity).
- **Claims:**
  1. Denial of paid FMLA leave from February 2021 to the present.
  2. Reassignment of a retired co-worker's complex cases to her on June 19, 2021.
  3. Denial of eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave on August 3, 2021.
  4. Denial of her final appeal of a reasonable accommodation request on August 24, 2021.
  5. Denial of her official time request on October 26, 2021.
- **Procedure:** After the investigation, the Agency gave Complainant the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing. She timely requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ.
- **Decision-maker:** The AJ issued a summary judgment decision for the Agency. The Agency then issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding that Complainant did not prove discrimination.

## Claims 1 and 3: FMLA leave
- **Prior decision:** In a prior EEO complaint, an EEOC AJ found on May 25, 2022 that the Agency had proven it placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021. Complainant had depleted her paid leave balances and failed to report to work. She raised the same February and March 2021 issues again in this complaint.
- **Supervisor1's account:**
  - Management's calculations showed Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021.
  - The Agency's February 26, 2021 FMLA letter said she had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021 and December 3, 2021.
  - On March 1, 2021 and other dates, Supervisor notified her she had no paid FMLA leave available. On various dates, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor granted FMLA-LWOP instead.
- **Audit:**
  - Complainant did not request an audit until August 5, 2021.
  - The audit, done by a payroll representative, showed she had some paid leave available.
  - Management then retroactively granted paid leave, including for August 3, 2021.
- **Complainant's statement:** She conceded she ultimately received all the paid leave she requested and was entitled to.
- **Comparators:** She identified no similarly situated employees treated more favorably.

## Claim 2: Reassignment of casework
- **Facts:** A GS-12 co-worker retired in June 2021. According to Complainant, Supervisor emailed her and two other GS-12 employees that the retired employee's cases would be split among the three.
- **Complainant's position:** She should not have received the cases because she had a pending reasonable accommodation request and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave.
- **Prior AJ finding:** An AJ found she was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency met all its Rehabilitation Act obligations. That appeal is pending (docket number removed). The record does not clearly say this was the prior case.
- **Supervisor's explanation:**
  - Assigning inventory was her job.
  - All the work was appropriate for Complainant's grade level.
  - The work was split among the three GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists by the alphabetical order of case names.
- **Documentary evidence:** The spreadsheet from Supervisor1 shows the case assignments.
- **Comparators:** The record contains no similarly situated employees treated more favorably.

## Claim 4: Reasonable accommodation
- **Requests:**
  - May 6, 2021: Complainant asked that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters, and for a reduced workload.
  - May 18, 2021: She amended the request to add reassignment.
  - She conceded her impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties.
- **Interactive meeting:** The Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with her on May 21, 2021.
- **Denial of reduced workload and reassignment (the Agency's reasons):**
  - There was no medical explanation supporting the need.
  - Lowering her caseload would lower performance or production standards and compromise the mission.
  - Her inventory was only 25 cases, well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below her typical caseload.
  - Reassignment is the accommodation of last resort, granted only when an employee cannot meet the essential functions of her position.
  - In a previous 2018 request, her psychologist had noted she desired roughly 38–40 cases.
  - When she requested reassignment in March 2020, she submitted no medical documentation showing she could not perform the essential functions. The evidence showed she wanted reassignment because of an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors.
- **Printer accommodation:**
  - The Agency approved a small portable printer, and management agreed to send her correspondence in the meantime.
  - Before delivery, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. She later averred she could not lift either the printer or its paper.
- **Appeal:**
  - The Agency denied her request for reconsideration.
  - She appealed on July 12, 2021.
  - On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations denied the appeal.
  - The Director's denial noted that she had summarily rejected the offered printer, already had a reduced workload, and was not eligible for reassignment because she could perform the essential functions of her job.

## Claim 5: Official time
- **Request:** On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested official time from about 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to complete an affidavit requested by the EEO Investigator.
- **Time used:** She used six hours on October 20 and four hours on October 21. She had not finished the affidavit and asked for more time on October 25.
- **October 25:** Supervisor approved additional official time that day.
- **October 26:**
  - Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension. OCRD responded that she could request an extension from the investigator.
  - She then asked Supervisor for more official time that day and said she had two questions remaining.
  - Supervisor denied the request. The stated reasons were that she had already received approximately 18 hours and that OCRD had told her to contact the investigator for an extension.

## AJ's summary judgment findings (decision-maker: AJ)
- **Hostile work environment:** The incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive.
- **Animus:** There was no evidence the conduct was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. Complainant did not show that similarly situated employees outside her protected classes were treated more favorably on FMLA or other leave.
- **Casework:** The reassigned cases were split equally among three Bankruptcy Specialists for unrebutted reasons of grade, skill level, and suitability given Complainant's low workload.
- **Accommodation:**
  - Complainant admitted her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties.
  - She offered no probative evidence that previously offered accommodations (a post of duty with telework away from her manager, and communication primarily by email) failed to let her perform the essential functions.
  - The record supported denying reduced inventory, because an agency need not change production standards such as lowering a case quota. She had an unusually low inventory of 25 cases and no evidence she could not perform her assignments.
  - After the interactive meeting, the Agency approved a lightweight portable printer. Management sent her correspondence meanwhile and continued to print and mail her letters after she cancelled the printer.
  - The AJ concluded the Agency did not deny reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act.
- **Official time:** The 18 hours granted was objectively reasonable to complete the affidavit despite the investigators' numerous questions. Her time was spent including information and documentation she had provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit official time to 18 hours and to have her seek more from the investigator.
- **Conclusion:** Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged.

## Outcome
The Agency issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding that Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged.

On April 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the basis of disability (physical- neck and shoulder) when: 1. Beginning on or about November 7, 2020 and ongoing, she was continually harassed (questioned) about her work restrictions and not provided work assistance; 2. Beginning on or about November 9, 2020, and continuing, she was required to do the walking portion of her route; 3. On December 23, 2020, she was yelled at and embarrassed in front of her coworkers; 4. On December 23, 2020, she was required to submit a new CA-17 and not paid for the time she missed from work to get the CA-17 completed; 5. On December 23, 2020, she was moved off Route 74 and required to case and carry Route 23; 6. On February 1, 2021, she was called to the supervisor’s desk to discuss her medical documents; 7. On March 23, 2021, she was harassed and referred to the District Reasonable Accommodation Committee (DRAC); 8. On April 2, 2021, her request for leave was not granted and she was charged Absent Without Leave (AWOL); and 9. On or about April 15, 2021, management gave her a modified assignment which changed her start time to 10:00 am and did not provide her with a mail cart. 2 The Agency dismissed a claim alleging that Complainant was attacked by a dog while on the job and not properly compensated for the time missed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) as a collateral attack on the Office of Workers’ Compensation (OWCP), which has jurisdiction over issues of compensation for work-related injuries. See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 71-75. We affirm the dismissal as the Commission has repeatedly stated that a complainant cannot use the EEO process to challenge actions which occurred during the OWCP adjudicatory process. See Janiece H. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC [number removed] (Jan. 8, 2016). The gravamen of Complainant’s claims amount to an allegation of a violation of the Rehabilitation Act because the Manager of Customer Service (Manager) subjected her to harassment based on her disability and forced her to work outside of her medical restrictions. Specifically, Complainant argues that the Manager marked her AWOL even though she had submitted a leave request which had been previously approved by the Supervisor of Customer Service (Supervisor), and that the Agency denied her a mail cart to help her with her duties. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing, but the AJ denied the hearing request as a sanction for Complainant’s failure to submit the required Preliminary Case Information and her failure to respond to the AJ’s Order to Show Cause. The AJ remanded the complaint to the Agency, and the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

**Complainant Position:** Carrier Technician at Agency's Garland-South Station, Garland, Texas

**Complaint Date:** April 17, 2021

**Basis of Complaint:** Discrimination on the basis of disability (physical—neck and shoulder)

---

## ALLEGATIONS

1. **Beginning on or about November 7, 2020 and ongoing:** Continual harassment (questioning) about work restrictions and no work assistance provided

2. **Beginning on or about November 9, 2020 and continuing:** Required to do the walking portion of her route

7. **March 23, 2021:** Harassed and referred to the District Reasonable Accommodation Committee (DRAC)

8. **April 2, 2021:** Leave request not granted and charged Absent Without Leave (AWOL)

9. **On or about April 15, 2021:** Given modified assignment with 10:00 am start time and no mail cart provided

A claim alleging Complainant was attacked by a dog while on the job and not properly compensated for missed time was dismissed pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) as a collateral attack on the Office of Workers' Compensation (OWCP). U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC [number removed], Jan. 8, 2016)

---

Violation of the Rehabilitation Act: Manager subjected Complainant to harassment based on disability and forced work outside medical restrictions, including:
- Marking Complainant AWOL despite prior approval of leave request by Supervisor of Customer Service
- Denial of mail cart to assist with duties

---

- Agency provided Complainant with Report of Investigation and notice of right to hearing before Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ)
- Complainant requested hearing
- AJ denied hearing request as sanction for failure to submit required Preliminary Case Information and failure to respond to AJ's Order to Show Cause
- AJ remanded complaint to Agency
- Agency issued final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b)

---

## FINAL DECISION

**Decision-Maker:** Agency

**Result:** Complainant failed to prove Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged
