# CASE FILE SUMMARY

## Complainant Position and Employment
Complainant worked as a City Carrier Technician, A-02/Q, at the Agency's Village Station in New York, New York. (Report of Investigation, Affidavit A at 190, Exhibit 1). The duties of a Carrier Technician included casing and delivering mail for several carrier routes, involving pushing, lifting, and simple grasping daily for eight hours a day. (ROI, Affidavit C2).

## Medical Background
Complainant's medical conditions stemmed from an on-the-job injury first diagnosed on May 10, 2014. (ROI at 64-65). Her diagnosed conditions included back sprain, displacement of lumbar intervertebral disc without myelopathy, and a hernia, which she had repaired after the on-the-job injury. (ROI, Complainant's Affidavit, at 191).

Complainant's medical restrictions included: sitting three hours, walking limited to 30 minutes, standing 10 minutes, avoiding reaching above the shoulder, twisting, bending, stooping, pushing, pulling, lifting, squatting, kneeling, and climbing. She also required 15-minute breaks every hour. (ROI at 191).

## Allegations

The complaint contained three main allegations:

1. **Assignment Outside Medical Restrictions and Payment Issues (Since June 26, 2016, and continuing)**: Management assigned Complainant work outside of her medical restrictions and failed to pay her properly and/or on time.

2. **Deleted Clock Rings (October 4, 2016, and other unspecified dates)**: Complainant's clock rings were deleted.

3. **Denied 204-B Detail (Unspecified dates)**: Complainant's request to be detailed as a 204-B acting supervisor was not granted.

## Modified Job Assignment

On June 22, 2016, an offer was not made to Complainant for a limited duty modified assignment to work at the Lenox Hill South Station from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. (ROI at 196, 233). The position was not a vacant, funded position. The assignment involved shuttling carriers by van to and from their routes and delivering express mail under five pounds for up to four hours a day and up to 30 minutes respectively. Complainant signed the modified job offer on July 1, 2016, and began the assignment on or about July 18, 2016. (ROI at 196, 233).

Complainant stated that although she felt the modified job assignment would be too much for her, she told her Manager that she would try it and let him know if she was unable to handle it, and he agreed. (ROI at 196).

The Manager testified that he became aware of Complainant's medical condition through the job offer. He denied receiving or having any medical documentation for Complainant.

## Alternative Accommodation Offered

The record shows that the Agency offered Complainant another light duty job as a lobby attendant. Complainant declined this position, believing it would be beyond what she could do given her restrictions.

On August 29, 2016, Complainant claimed she walked an hour (with breaks), even though she was not supposed to walk more than 30 minutes, and was not permitted the use of the van. (ROI at 196).

## Clock Ring Deletions and Payment Errors

Complainant's clock rings were deleted for dates July 18, 2016, through July 28, 2016, and her time was coded as full workers' compensation. (ROI, Affidavit A). Complainant had just started working at the Lenox Hill Station and the receiving station should have entered her time.

The Manager averred that Complainant had an incorrect leave code in the system. (ROI, Affidavit B).

Complainant was out on leave for significant periods in July and August 2016 and did not return to work until October 4, 2016, to fill out workers' compensation paperwork and again on November 14, 2016, to fill out additional paperwork. Because Complainant switched from Village Station to Lenox Hill, there is insufficient evidence that the supervisor at the receiving facility realized she had returned to work from being out on workers' compensation.

Complainant asserted that her Manager's poor organization was another reason for the errors made. (ROI at 197-198 (209-210)).

On September 14, 2016, Complainant filed a grievance regarding the payment failures and the deleted clock rings. The Agency maintained that the payment failures were due to plain error.

The record shows that manual timecards had been submitted and lost. Complainant believed errors may have been caused by the Agency not having a disk which would have allowed automatic logging of hours rather than manual submission.

## 204-B Detail Request

On or about November 14, 2016, Complainant requested to serve as an acting supervisor (204-B) over the carriers. The Manager did not offer her a 204-B detail as a reasonable accommodation. (ROI, Affidavit B). The Manager averred he did not need any acting supervisors for his operations and believed that supervisors must be punctual and reliable, attributes he did not observe in Complainant. (ROI, Affidavit B).

Complainant claimed the Manager and another manager "brushed her off." Complainant stated that instead of training her for a 204-B position, she was told she could apply for a city-wide position that would take time to obtain.

## Agency Dismissal and Investigation Conclusion

The Agency dismissed an additional claim for failure to state a claim. Complainant raised no challenges regarding this matter.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge.

## Administrative Judge Decision

Complainant timely requested a hearing. The assigned Administrative Judge (AJ) issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency, finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged.

**Claim (1) - Reasonable Accommodation and Work Outside Restrictions:**

The AJ determined that Complainant was provided a modified limited duty assignment of shuttling carriers in a van and delivering express mail which was within her documented medical restrictions. The AJ noted that Complainant believed the job was too much for her. The Agency offered Complainant another modified assignment of lobby attendant, which she declined. The AJ noted that Complainant claimed another modified assignment that was offered and rescinded would have met her needs, but that position contained similar tasks as the lobby attendant position that she declined.

The AJ determined there was no evidence that Complainant was forced to work outside of her medical restrictions. The AJ found that Complainant appeared to have been unable to perform her job with or without a reasonable accommodation as her medical restrictions were so severe. The AJ concluded that Complainant was not denied reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act.

**Claims (2) and (3) - Clock Ring Deletions, Payment Issues, and 204-B Detail:**

The AJ determined that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. With respect to claims that Complainant was not paid properly and her clock rings were deleted, Agency officials explained errors occurred for several reasons: Complainant returned to full-time duty from workers' compensation so supervisors at the other facility may not have realized she had returned to work; Complainant switched from one facility to another; manual timecards were submitted and lost instead of digital submission which would have prevented the issue; and Complainant herself noted that the Manager had poor organizational skills which contributed to the errors.

As to the 204-B detail claim, the AJ determined that Complainant wanted a manager to promote her on the spot rather than actually applying for the detail assignment. The AJ found that Complainant failed to show that the denial of the detail was a result of discriminatory or retaliatory animus and failed to show that the Agency's reasons for its actions were pretextual.

The AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged.

## Final Agency Order

The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ's decision. This appeal followed.

The AJ assigned to the case issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency finding that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. In the decision, the AJ found that Complainant was not denied reasonable accommodation as alleged in claim (1). The AJ determined that Complainant was provided a modified limited duty assignment of shuttling carriers in a van and delivering express mail which was within her documented medical restrictions. Complainant believed that the job was too much for her. The Agency offered Complainant another modified assignment of lobby attendant, but she declined the position. The AJ noted that Complainant claimed another modified assignment that was offered and rescinded would have met her needs, but that position contained similar tasks as the lobby attendant position that she declined. The AJ determined that there was no evidence that Complainant was forced to work outside of her medical restrictions. Thus, Complainant appeared to have been unable to perform her job with or without a reasonable accommodation as her medical restrictions were so severe. Therefore, the AJ found that Complainant was not denied reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. With respect to the remaining issues, the AJ determined that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. More specifically, with respect to her claims that she was not paid properly and her clock rings were deleted, Agency officials explained that errors occurred for a number or reasons. For example, Complainant returned to full-time duty from workers’ compensation so supervisors at the other facility may not have realized she had returned to work. In addition, Complainant switched from one facility to another. Another reason was because manual timecards were submitted and lost instead of digital submission which would have prevented the issue. Finally, Complainant herself noted that the Manager had poor organizational skills which contributed to the errors. As to her claim that her request to be detailed as a 204-B acting supervisor was not granted, Complainant claimed that the Manager and another manager “brushed her off” and that she mentioned the detail as a way for her to be accommodated. The Manager offered her the two above-discussed positions as accommodations. Complainant stated that instead of training her for a 204-B position, she was told she could apply for a city-wide position that would take time to obtain. The AJ determined that Complainant wanted a manager to promote her on the spot rather than actually applying for the detail assignment. The AJ found that Complainant failed to show that the denial of the detail was a result of discriminatory or retaliatory animus. The AJ concluded that Complainant failed to show that the Agency’s reasons for its actions were pretextual. As a result, the AJ found that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination or reprisal as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting the AJ’s decision. This appeal followed.

# Case File Summary

## Parties and Claims
Complainant was a City Carrier Technician, A-02/Q, at the Agency's Village Station in New York, New York (Report of Investigation (ROI), Affidavit A at 190, Exhibit 1). She alleged the following:
1. Since June 27, 2016, and continuing, management assigned her work outside her medical restrictions and failed to pay her properly and/or on time.
2. On October 4, 2016, and other unspecified dates, her clock rings were deleted.
3. On unspecified dates, her request to be detailed as a 204-B was not granted.

## Background
- **Duties:** A Carrier Technician cases and delivers mail for several carrier routes. The duties include pushing, lifting, and simple grasping daily for eight hours a day (ROI, Affidavit C2).
- **Medical conditions:** Complainant attributes her conditions to a recurrence of an on-the-job injury. Her physician noted May 10, 2014, as the date of injury and first diagnosis (ROI at 64-65). She averred that her conditions are a back sprain, displacement of lumbar intervertebral disc without myelopathy, and a hernia that was repaired after the injury (ROI, Complainant's Affidavit, at 191).
- **Restrictions:**
  - Sitting three hours.
  - Walking limited to 30 minutes.
  - Standing 10 minutes.
  - Avoiding reaching above the shoulder, twisting, bending, stooping, pushing, pulling, lifting, squatting, kneeling, and climbing.
  - 15-minute breaks every hour (ROI at 191).
- **Return from leave:** After an extended leave, she was assigned to the Lenox Hill Station.

## Modified Assignment (Claim 1)
- **Offer:** On June 22, 2016, Complainant was offered a limited duty modified assignment at Lenox Hill South Station, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The position was not a vacant, funded position. It involved shuttling carriers by van to and from their routes (up to four hours a day) and delivering express mail under five pounds (up to 30 minutes). On paper, it met her restrictions.
- **Acceptance:** She signed the offer on July 1, 2016, and began on or about July 18, 2016 (ROI at 196, 233).
- **Complainant's statements:** She felt the assignment would be too much but told her Manager she would try it and tell him if she could not handle it. He agreed (ROI at 196).
- **Complainant's claims:**
  - On August 29, 2016, she walked an hour (with breaks), though she was not to walk more than 30 minutes.
  - She was not permitted to use the van.
  - Using the van, as the offer indicated, would require stooping and twisting.
  - Even picking up a dropped envelope would violate her restriction on stooping (ROI at 196).
- **Manager's statements:** He testified that he learned of her medical condition through the job offer. He denied receiving or having any medical documentation for her. The record states it is undisputed that he instructed her to make an express delivery, which he believed conformed to her restrictions (ROI at 196).
- **Other offer:** Complainant was offered a light duty lobby attendant job. She declined it because she believed it was beyond her restrictions.
- **Leave:** The record shows she was on leave for significant periods in July and August 2016.

## Pay and Clock Rings (Claims 1 and 2)
- Some clock rings for July 18, 2016, through July 28, 2016, were deleted, and her time was coded as full workers' compensation. The record states that the receiving station should have entered her time (ROI, Affidavit A).
- The Manager averred that she had an incorrect leave code in the system (ROI, Affidavit B).
- She returned to work on October 4, 2016, and again on November 14, 2016, only to complete workers' compensation paperwork.
- She had recently returned from full-time workers' compensation and had moved from the Village Station to Lenox Hill. The record states there is insufficient evidence that the receiving supervisor realized she had returned to work.
- Complainant asserted that her Manager's poor organization was another reason for the errors (ROI at 197-198 (209-210)).
- The deletion of the clock rings was discovered before the EEO filing at issue. On September 14, 2016, she filed a grievance about the payment failures and deleted clock rings.
- The Agency maintained that the payment failures were due to plain error.
- Manual timecards were submitted and lost. Complainant cited the errors and believed they may have resulted from the Agency not having a disk that would let her log hours automatically.

## 204-B Detail (Claim 3)
- Complainant averred that she asked to serve as an acting supervisor (204-B). On or about November 14, 2016, the Manager did not offer her a 204-B detail as a reasonable accommodation.
- The Manager averred that he did not need any acting supervisors. He also averred that supervisors must be punctual and reliable, and that he did not observe those attributes in Complainant (ROI, Affidavit B).

## Dismissed Claim
The Agency dismissed an additional claim for failure to state a claim. Complainant raised no challenge, and the Commission found no basis to disturb the dismissal.

## Procedural History and Decision
- After the investigation, the Agency gave Complainant the ROI and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). She timely requested a hearing.
- **Decision-maker:** The AJ issued a summary judgment decision for the Agency, finding no discrimination or reprisal.
- **Criteria applied:**
  - Reasonable accommodation under the Rehabilitation Act (claim 1).
  - For the remaining issues, whether the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons, and whether Complainant showed pretext, including discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

### AJ's findings
- **Claim 1, accommodation:**
  - The modified assignment of shuttling carriers by van and delivering express mail was within her documented restrictions. Complainant believed it was too much.
  - She declined the lobby attendant assignment.
  - She claimed that another assignment, offered and rescinded, would have met her needs. The AJ found it contained tasks similar to the lobby attendant position she declined.
  - There was no evidence she was forced to work outside her restrictions.
  - The AJ stated that Complainant appeared unable to perform her job with or without reasonable accommodation because her restrictions were so severe.
  - The AJ found no denial of reasonable accommodation under the Rehabilitation Act.
- **Pay and clock rings:** Agency officials gave several explanations for the errors:
  - She returned from workers' compensation, so supervisors at the other facility may not have known.
  - She switched facilities.
  - Manual timecards were submitted and lost instead of digital submission.
  - Complainant herself noted the Manager's poor organizational skills.
- **204-B detail:**
  - Complainant claimed the Manager and another manager "brushed her off." She said she raised the detail as a way to be accommodated.
  - She stated that, instead of being trained for a 204-B position, she was told she could apply for a city-wide position that would take time to obtain.
  - The Manager offered her the two positions discussed above as accommodations.
  - The AJ determined that she wanted to be promoted on the spot rather than apply for the detail. The AJ found she did not show that the denial resulted from discriminatory or retaliatory animus.
- **Pretext:** The AJ concluded that Complainant failed to show the Agency's reasons were pretextual.

The Agency issued a final order fully adopting the AJ's decision. This appeal followed.

## Gaps in the Record
The excerpt does not give the dates of the hearing request, the AJ's decision, or the final order. It also does not name the Manager or give a record citation for the Manager's testimony about medical documentation.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

**Parties and Positions:**
Complainant worked as a Deportation Officer (DO), GS-12, at the Agency's office in San Bernardino, California. His first-line supervisor was a Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer (Vietnamese; YOB: 1977; no prior EEO activity). (ROI at 76)

**Alleged Discriminatory Acts:**

**Claim 1 – July 26, 2018: Denial of Schedule Adjustment Request**
Complainant alleged Supervisor denied his request to attend a concert with his daughter and to adjust his DO 1's schedule. (ROI at 13-14, 47, 120)

Supervisor's account: On July 27, 2018, Complainant requested via text to adjust his schedule to 0500-1300 hours to attend a recreational event. Supervisor stated he informed Complainant the earliest he could come in was 0600 or Complainant could use Annual Leave. Supervisor recalled Complainant informed him via text he would take leave; however, Complainant decided to report to work. (ROI at 77-80, 90)

**Claim 2 – July 27, 2018: Request to Return to Work**
Complainant stated Supervisor asked him to return to work after he had already left for the day. (ROI at 13-14)

Supervisor's account: He asked Complainant to come to his office during Complainant's duty hours. Complainant continued working the remaining hours and then worked overtime from 4:30 p.m. until 7:00 p.m. (ROI at 80-82, 91) The record reflected Complainant claimed work hours from 0500 to 1900 on the date at issue—eight hours regular pay and six hours of Administrative Uncontrollable Overtime (AUO). (ROI at 91, 137)

**Claim 3 – October 1, 2018: Pay Discrepancies**
Complainant asserted he became aware of pay discrepancies made by Supervisor on October 1, 2018. Complainant also claimed Supervisor had informed DO 2 (YOB: 1969; prior EEO activity; national origin unknown) of DO 2's AUO pay discrepancy prior to correcting DO 2's pay. (ROI at 13-14, 47, 120)

Supervisor's account: On October 4, 2018, Complainant and the Union President came to his office claiming Complainant had worked AUO from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on August 28, 2018. Supervisor explained Complainant could not claim AUO during the hour he was in training from 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., as it was excludable from AUO; accordingly, Supervisor had made the pay adjustment. (ROI at 83-85, 93) On August 28, 2018, Complainant was in an all-day Defensive Tactics training class scheduled from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Supervisor asserted DO 2 had been available in the office when Supervisor discovered the AUO discrepancy, and therefore, Supervisor was able to discuss the change with DO 2. Supervisor denied treating Complainant differently based on Complainant's protected classes. (ROI at 84-85)

**Claim 4 – October 12, 2018: Performance Work Plan Review**
Complainant asserted Supervisor admonished him several times in his Performance Work Plan (PWP) and rated him in an area which was not in his official PWP. (ROI at 13, 47)

Supervisor's account: On October 12, 2018, Supervisor reviewed Complainant's PWP with him. Supervisor stated Complainant became upset and walked away, which negated the opportunity for discussion. (ROI at 86-87, 98-110) Supervisor stated, and the record showed, that he rated Complainant on the following elements: Plans and Conducts Arrest, Custody Operations, Deportation, Partnering, Prepares Reports and Other Correspondence. Supervisor maintained he did not rate Complainant on elements that were not on Complainant's PWP. (ROI at 86-87, 98-110)

**EEO Complaint Filing:**
Complainant initiated EEO contact on October 12, 2018. On June 6, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to a hostile work environment on the bases of national origin (Romanian), age (48; YOB: 1971), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (HS-ICE-21417-2012 and HS-ICE-22663-2012) under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967.

**Administrative Proceedings:**
On June 7, 2021, the assigned Administrative Judge (AJ) issued an Order to Show Good Cause as Complainant failed to provide a completed investigative affidavit in response to the EEO investigator's multiple requests and failed to file the affidavit pursuant to an AJ order issued on May 11, 2021. The AJ ordered Complainant to provide a statement by June 17, 2021 stating why there was good cause for failing to submit the completed affidavit. On June 21, 2021, Complainant emailed the AJ stating his apologies but still provided no affidavit. On June 22, 2021, the AJ dismissed the complaint from the EEOC hearing process and remanded it to the Agency to issue a Final Agency Decision (FAD) as a sanction for Complainant's failure to comply with the AJ's orders.

**Final Agency Decision:**
On August 10, 2021, the Agency issued a FAD pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).

**Analysis and Conclusions:**
The Agency concluded Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

For claims 1, 3, and 4 (disparate treatment allegations), the Agency analyzed the claims under the three-part evidentiary scheme from McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973) and determined that management articulated legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons for the challenged actions:

- **Claim 1:** Supervisor stated Complainant did not request time off but decided to report to work and that Complainant was not treated differently than DO 1. (ROI at 77-80)
- **Claim 3:** Supervisor asserted DO 2 had been available in the office when Supervisor discovered the AUO discrepancy, allowing discussion with DO 2. Supervisor denied treating Complainant differently based on protected classes. (ROI at 84-85)
- **Claim 4:** Supervisor asserted he did not admonish Complainant in his PWP or rate him in areas not included on the PWP. (ROI at 86-87, 98-110)

The Agency found Complainant failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that management's legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons were pretexts for discrimination, nor did Complainant provide evidence the Agency's actions were based on his protected classes.

For claims including the non-discrete allegation raised in claim 2 and discrete acts in remaining claims, the Agency analyzed them under the legal standard for harassment and found Complainant failed to prove the Agency subjected him to an unlawful, discriminatory, hostile work environment. The record did not contain evidence demonstrating management's actions were motivated by discriminatory intent or that Complainant was subjected to unwelcome conduct based on membership in a protected class. Complainant's allegations did not constitute the kind of severe or pervasive harassment that Title VII was designed to prevent. The Agency concluded Complainant failed to prove management's actions bore a relationship to his claimed protected bases and that there was no evidence the alleged harassing conduct was based on those protected bases or on discriminatory animus.

**Appeal:**
This appeal followed; however, neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted an appeal statement.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

**Parties and Positions:**
Complainant worked as a Deportation Officer (DO), GS-12, at the Agency's office in San Bernardino, California. His first-line supervisor was a Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer (Vietnamese; YOB: 1977; no prior EEO activity). (ROI at 76)

**Alleged Discriminatory Acts:**

**Claim 1 – July 27, 2018: Denial of Schedule Adjustment Request**
Complainant alleged Supervisor denied his request to attend a concert with his daughter and to adjust his DO 1's schedule. (ROI at 13-14, 47, 120)

Supervisor's account: On July 27, 2018, Complainant requested via text to adjust his schedule to 0500-1300 hours to attend a recreational event. Supervisor stated he informed Complainant the earliest he could come in was 0600 or Complainant could use Annual Leave. Supervisor recalled Complainant informed him via text he would take leave; however, Complainant decided to report to work. (ROI at 77-80, 90)

**Claim 2 – July 27, 2018: Request to Return to Work**
Complainant stated Supervisor asked him to return to work after he had already left for the day. (ROI at 13-14)

Supervisor's account: He asked Complainant to come to his office during Complainant's duty hours. Complainant continued working the remaining hours and then worked overtime from 4:30 p.m. until 7:00 p.m. (ROI at 80-82, 91) The record reflected Complainant claimed work hours from 0500 to 1900 on the date at issue—eight hours regular pay and six hours of Administrative Uncontrollable Overtime (AUO). (ROI at 91, 137)

**Claim 3 – October 1, 2018: Pay Discrepancies**
Complainant asserted he became aware of pay discrepancies made by Supervisor on October 1, 2018. Complainant also claimed Supervisor had informed DO 2 (YOB: 1969; prior EEO activity; national origin unknown) of DO 2's AUO pay discrepancy prior to correcting DO 2's pay. (ROI at 13-14, 47, 120)

Supervisor's account: On October 4, 2018, Complainant and the Union President came to his office claiming Complainant had worked AUO from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on August 28, 2018. Supervisor explained Complainant could not claim AUO during the hour he was in training from 3:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., as it was excludable from AUO; accordingly, Supervisor had made the pay adjustment. (ROI at 83-85, 93) On August 28, 2018, Complainant was in an all-day Defensive Tactics training class scheduled from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Supervisor asserted DO 2 had been available in the office when Supervisor discovered the AUO discrepancy, and therefore, Supervisor was able to discuss the change with DO 2. Supervisor denied treating Complainant differently based on Complainant's protected classes. (ROI at 84-85)

**Claim 4 – October 12, 2018: Performance Work Plan Review**
Complainant asserted Supervisor admonished him several times in his Performance Work Plan (PWP) and rated him in an area which was not in his official PWP. (ROI at 13, 47)

Supervisor's account: On October 12, 2018, Supervisor reviewed Complainant's PWP with him. Supervisor stated Complainant became upset and walked away, which negated the opportunity for discussion. (ROI at 86-87, 98-110) Supervisor stated, and the record showed, that he rated Complainant on the following elements: Plans and Conducts Arrest, Custody Operations, Deportation, Partnering, Prepares Reports and Other Correspondence. Supervisor maintained he did not rate Complainant on elements that were not on Complainant's PWP. (ROI at 86-87, 98-110)

**EEO Complaint Filing:**
Complainant initiated EEO contact on October 12, 2018. On June 6, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to a hostile work environment on the bases of national origin (Romanian), age (48; YOB: 1971), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (HS-ICE-21417-2012 and HS-ICE-22663-2012) under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967.

**Administrative Proceedings:**
On June 7, 2021, the assigned Administrative Judge (AJ) issued an Order to Show Good Cause as Complainant failed to provide a completed investigative affidavit in response to the EEO investigator's multiple requests and failed to file the affidavit pursuant to an AJ order issued on May 11, 2021. The AJ ordered Complainant to provide a statement by June 17, 2021 stating why there was good cause for failing to submit the completed affidavit. On June 21, 2021, Complainant emailed the AJ stating his apologies but still provided no affidavit. On June 22, 2021, the AJ dismissed the complaint from the EEOC hearing process and remanded it to the Agency to issue a Final Agency Decision (FAD) as a sanction for Complainant's failure to comply with the AJ's orders.

**Final Agency Decision:**
On August 10, 2021, the Agency issued a FAD pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).

**Analysis and Conclusions:**
The Agency concluded Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

For claims 1, 3, and 4 (disparate treatment allegations), the Agency analyzed the claims under the three-part evidentiary scheme from McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973) and determined that management articulated legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons for the challenged actions:

- **Claim 1:** Supervisor stated Complainant did not request time off but decided to report to work and that Complainant was not treated differently than DO 1. (ROI at 77-80)
- **Claim 3:** Supervisor asserted DO 2 had been available in the office when Supervisor discovered the AUO discrepancy, allowing discussion with DO 2. Supervisor denied treating Complainant differently based on protected classes. (ROI at 84-85)
- **Claim 4:** Supervisor asserted he did not admonish Complainant in his PWP or rate him in areas not included on the PWP. (ROI at 86-87, 98-110)

The Agency found Complainant failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that management's legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons were pretexts for discrimination, nor did Complainant provide evidence the Agency's actions were based on his protected classes.

For claims including the non-discrete allegation raised in claim 2 and discrete acts in remaining claims, the Agency analyzed them under the legal standard for harassment and found Complainant failed to prove the Agency subjected him to an unlawful, discriminatory, hostile work environment. The record did not contain evidence demonstrating management's actions were motivated by discriminatory intent or that Complainant was subjected to unwelcome conduct based on membership in a protected class. Complainant's allegations did not constitute the kind of severe or pervasive harassment that Title VII was designed to prevent. The Agency concluded Complainant failed to prove management's actions bore a relationship to his claimed protected bases and that there was no evidence the alleged harassing conduct was based on those protected bases or on discriminatory animus.

**Appeal:**
This appeal followed; however, neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted an appeal statement.

  - DO 1: YOB 1982; no prior EEO activity; national origin unknown.
  - DO 2: YOB 1969; prior EEO activity; national origin unknown.

- **October 12, 2018:** Complainant initiated EEO contact.
- **June 6, 2019:** Complainant filed the EEO complaint.
- The Agency investigated and gave Complainant the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing.
- **May 11, 2021:** The AJ issued an order directing Complainant to file an investigative affidavit. Complainant did not comply, despite the EEO investigator's multiple requests.

- **August 10, 2021:** The Agency issued the FAD under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).
- Complainant then appealed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted an appeal statement.

## Claims and the Evidence in the Record

**Claim 1 – July 26, 2018: Supervisor denied Complainant's request to attend a concert with his daughter.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13-14, 47, 120): Supervisor denied the request. He also alleged disparate treatment relative to DO 1 regarding schedule adjustment.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 77-80, 90):
  - On July 27, 2018, Complainant texted a request to adjust his schedule to 0500-1300 to attend a recreational event.
  - Supervisor replied that the earliest Complainant could start was 0600, or he could use Annual Leave.
  - Complainant texted that he would take leave but then decided to report to work.

**Claim 2 – July 27, 2018: Supervisor asked Complainant to return to work after he had already left for the day.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13-4): He had already left for the day when Supervisor asked him to return.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 80-2, 91): He asked Complainant to come to his office during Complainant's duty hours. Complainant continued working the remaining hours, then worked overtime from 4:30 p.m. to 7:00 p.m.

- *Complainant* (ROI at 13-4, 47, 120): Supervisor told DO 2 of DO 2's Administrative Uncontrollable Overtime (AUO) pay discrepancy before correcting DO 2's pay.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 83-5, 93):
  - On October 4, 2018, Complainant and the Union President came to his office claiming Complainant had worked AUO from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on August 28, 2018.
  - On that date Complainant was in all-day Defensive Tactics training, scheduled from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  - Supervisor explained that the 3-4 p.m. training hour was excludable from AUO, and he made the pay adjustment accordingly.

**Claim 4 – October 12, 2018: Supervisor admonished Complainant several times in his Performance Work Plan (PWP) and rated him in an area not in his official PWP.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13, 47): Supervisor admonished him several times in the PWP and rated him on an area not in his official PWP.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 86-7, 98-110):
  - He reviewed the PWP with Complainant on October 12, 2018.
  - Complainant became upset and walked away, which ended any opportunity for discussion.
  - Supervisor rated Complainant only on elements in his PWP: Plans and Conducts Arrest, Custody Operations, Deportation, Partnering, and Prepares Reports and Other Correspondence.
  - The record also showed these were the elements rated (ROI at 86-7, 98-110).

## Agency Decision (FAD, August 10, 2021)
**Decision-maker:** The Agency, issuing the FAD after the AJ's remand. **Finding:** Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged.

**Disparate treatment (claims 1, 3, 4):**
- **Criteria:** The three-part evidentiary scheme of *McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green*, 411 U.S. 792 (1973).
- **Conclusion:** Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons. Complainant did not prove by a preponderance of the evidence that these were pretext, and he provided no evidence that the actions were based on his protected classes.
- **Responses considered:**
  - Claim 1: Supervisor's statement that Complainant did not request time off but decided to report to work, and that Complainant was not treated differently than DO 1 (ROI at 77-80).
  - Claim 3: Supervisor's assertion that DO 2 was available in the office when the AUO discrepancy was found, so Supervisor could discuss the change with DO 2. Supervisor denied treating Complainant differently based on his protected classes (ROI at 84-5).
  - Claim 4: Supervisor's assertion that he did not admonish Complainant in the PWP or rate him in areas not in his PWP.

**Harassment / hostile work environment (claim 2 as a non-discrete allegation, plus the discrete acts in the other claims):**
- **Criteria:** The legal standard for harassment.
- **Conclusion:** Complainant failed to prove an unlawful, discriminatory hostile work environment.
- **Reasoning:**
  - The record contained no evidence that management's actions were motivated by discriminatory intent or that Complainant was subjected to unwelcome conduct based on a protected class.
  - The allegations did not amount to the severe or pervasive harassment Title VII was designed to prevent.
  - Management's actions bore no relationship to the claimed protected bases.
  - There was no evidence that the alleged conduct was based on those bases, and no discriminatory animus.

## Notes for the File
- The record gives no year for the AJ's June 22 dismissal.
- The record gives no date for the appeal.
- Claim 1 is dated July 26, 2018 in the complaint, but Supervisor's account of the schedule request refers to July 27, 2018.
- The FAD's analysis of claim 4 cites no ROI pages in the record.

- **June 21, 2021:** Complainant emailed the AJ with apologies but still provided no affidavit.
- **June 22:** The AJ dismissed the complaint from the hearing process and remanded it to the Agency for a Final Agency Decision (FAD), as a sanction for noncompliance with the AJ's orders.
- **August 10, 2021:** The Agency issued the FAD under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).
- Complainant then appealed. Neither Complainant nor the Agency submitted an appeal statement.

## Claims and the Evidence in the Record

**Claim 1 – July 26, 2018: Supervisor denied Complainant's request to attend a concert with his daughter.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13-14, 47, 120): Supervisor denied the request. He also alleged disparate treatment relative to DO 1 regarding schedule adjustment.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 77-80, 90):
  - On July 27, 2018, Complainant texted a request to adjust his schedule to 0500-1300 to attend a recreational event.
  - Supervisor replied that the earliest Complainant could start was 0600, or he could use Annual Leave.
  - Complainant texted that he would take leave but then decided to report to work.

**Claim 2 – July 27, 2018: Supervisor asked Complainant to return to work after he had already left for the day.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13-4): He had already left for the day when Supervisor asked him to return.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 80-2, 91): He asked Complainant to come to his office during Complainant's duty hours. Complainant continued working the remaining hours, then worked overtime from 4:30 p.m. to 7:00 p.m.
- *Record* (ROI at 91, 137): On that date Complainant claimed work hours from 0500 to 1900, consisting of eight hours of regular pay and six hours of AUO.

**Claim 3 – October 1, 2018: Complainant became aware of pay discrepancies made by Supervisor.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13-4, 47, 120): Supervisor told DO 2 of DO 2's Administrative Uncontrollable Overtime (AUO) pay discrepancy before correcting DO 2's pay.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 83-5, 93):
  - On October 4, 2018, Complainant and the Union President came to his office claiming Complainant had worked AUO from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on August 28, 2018.
  - On that date Complainant was in all-day Defensive Tactics training, scheduled from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  - Supervisor explained that the 3-4 p.m. training hour was excludable from AUO, and he made the pay adjustment accordingly.

**Claim 4 – October 12, 2018: Supervisor admonished Complainant several times in his Performance Work Plan (PWP) and rated him in an area not in his official PWP.**
- *Complainant* (ROI at 13, 47): Supervisor admonished him several times in the PWP and rated him on an area not in his official PWP.
- *Supervisor* (ROI at 86-7, 98-110):
  - He reviewed the PWP with Complainant on October 12, 2018.
  - Complainant became upset and walked away, which ended any opportunity for discussion.
  - Supervisor rated Complainant only on elements in his PWP: Plans and Conducts Arrest, Custody Operations, Deportation, Partnering, and Prepares Reports and Other Correspondence.
  - The record also showed these were the elements rated (ROI at 86-7, 98-110).

## Agency Decision (FAD, August 10, 2021)
**Decision-maker:** The Agency, issuing the FAD after the AJ's remand. **Finding:** Complainant failed to prove discrimination as alleged.

**Disparate treatment (claims 1, 3, 4):**
- **Criteria:** The three-part evidentiary scheme of *McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green*, 411 U.S. 792 (1973).
- **Conclusion:** Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons. Complainant did not prove by a preponderance of the evidence that these were pretext, and he provided no evidence that the actions were based on his protected classes.
- **Responses considered:**
  - Claim 1: Supervisor's statement that Complainant did not request time off but decided to report to work, and that Complainant was not treated differently than DO 1 (ROI at 77-80).
  - Claim 3: Supervisor's assertion that DO 2 was available in the office when the AUO discrepancy was found, so Supervisor could discuss the change with DO 2. Supervisor denied treating Complainant differently based on his protected classes (ROI at 84-5).
  - Claim 4: Supervisor's assertion that he did not admonish Complainant in the PWP or rate him in areas not in his PWP.

**Harassment / hostile work environment (claim 2 as a non-discrete allegation, plus the discrete acts in the other claims):**
- **Criteria:** The legal standard for harassment.
- **Conclusion:** Complainant failed to prove an unlawful, discriminatory hostile work environment.
- **Reasoning:**
  - The record contained no evidence that management's actions were motivated by discriminatory intent or that Complainant was subjected to unwelcome conduct based on a protected class.
  - The allegations did not amount to the severe or pervasive harassment Title VII was designed to prevent.
  - Management's actions bore no relationship to the claimed protected bases.
  - There was no evidence that the alleged conduct was based on those bases, and no discriminatory animus.

## Notes for the File
- The record gives no year for the AJ's June 22 dismissal.
- The record gives no date for the appeal.
- Claim 1 is dated July 26, 2018 in the complaint, but Supervisor's account of the schedule request refers to July 27, 2018.
- The FAD's analysis of claim 4 cites no ROI pages in the record.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

## COMPLAINANT AND POSITION
Complainant was employed as a Customs and Border Protection Officer (CBPO) at the San Ysidro Port of Entry in San Ysidro, California, with Year of Birth 1954.

## ALLEGATIONS
Complainant alleged discrimination based on age (under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967) and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964).

## HARASSMENT ALLEGATIONS (Beginning May 31, 2018 and Continuing)

**May 31, 2018:** The Branch Chief refused to rescind a Memorandum of Counseling regarding Treasury Enforcement Communication System (TECS) that Complainant received. (ROI at 205)

**February 2019 to June 2019:** The Branch Chief was aware that the Supervisory CBP Officer (SCBPO-1) bullied and harassed Complainant yet took no corrective actions. (ROI at 205)

**April 17, 2019:** SCBPO-1 verbally reprimanded Complainant for missing a morning training class. (ROI at 205)

**June 2019:** SCBPO-1 showed a knife to Complainant and another CBPO (CBPO-2) and informed them that he brings his knife collection to work in his backpack. (ROI at 205)

**June 3, 2019:** SCBPO-1 reprimanded Complainant by email regarding his TECS access expiring. (ROI at 205)

**June 19, 2019:** SCBPO-1 changed Complainant's schedule from 2:00 p.m. to 1:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. in order to celebrate the Chief's birthday, and solicited $20 from him for the birthday party. (ROI at 205)

**On or around August 16, 2019:** SCBPO-1 and another SCBPO (SCBPO-2) informed Complainant's coworkers that he would be reassigned and leaving the Intelligence Targeting Unit effective September 1, 2019, although Complainant was not reassigned at that time. (ROI at 205)

**On or around August 16, 2019:** SCBPO-1 and SCBPO-2 informed Complainant that his request for leave during the month of September 2019 would not be approved; however, after Complainant questioned them about the matter, his leave was ultimately approved. (ROI at 205)

## REMOVAL FROM DETAIL
**Effective March 8, 2020:** Complainant was removed from his detail in the Intelligence Targeting Unit (ITU). (ROI at 205)

## DISMISSED CLAIMS
The Agency dismissed two claims: (1) that on December 23, 2018, Complainant learned he had not received a year-end monetary award; and (2) that on April 21, 2019, SCBPO-1 charged Complainant with 1 hour of Leave Without Pay for untimely counselor contact. (ROI at 150-57)

The Agency dismissed three claims alleging that SCBPO-1 was unprofessional in speaking ill about three coworkers for failure to state a claim, as Complainant did not show that he was aggrieved by comments made about other employees. (ROI at 150-57)

## AGENCY'S STATED JUSTIFICATIONS

**Memorandum of Counseling (May 31, 2018):**
The Branch Chief stated that she requested that Complainant be issued the Memorandum of Counseling after he was twice instructed not to put the terms "E/O if not in vehicle" on a TECS record as it creates a violation and Complainant continued not to comply. (ROI at 205)

The Intelligence Division Chief (CID Chief) explained that Complainant requested CBPOs to "exempt" travelers on primary which had illegal activity links/ties or which he targeted for illegal activity, which was essentially asking CBPOs to violate TECS policy. The CID Chief approved the issuance of the Memorandum of Counseling due to Complainant's failure to follow instructions even after being asked twice to do so. (ROI at 259)

**June 3, 2019 TECS Access Email:**
SCBPO-1 explained that the TECS system sends automated periodic reminders when a user is required to recertify in order to maintain their access from 30 days prior to the due date of recertification. (ROI at 223-24)

SCBPO-1 stated that he received an automated email from the TECS system informing him that Complainant had lost his access and he sent Complainant an email counseling him on the loss of access and reminding Complainant that he was required to maintain TECS access. (ROI at 223-24)

**June 19, 2019 Schedule Change and Birthday Solicitation:**
SCBPO-1 explained that the ITU had a tradition of organizing "potlucks" or obtaining catering for the group for certain situations and that such events are announced as optional participation. (ROI at 224)

SCBPO-1 stated that he told the ITU employees that the potluck would be held at 1:00 p.m. and that the 2:00 p.m. shift was told they could come in an hour early in order to participate. (ROI at 224)

SCBPO-1 stated that each employee was asked to donate $10 if they wished to and that CBPO-1 gave him $20 to pay for both himself and Complainant after Complainant verbally told him that he wished to participate. (ROI at 224)

**Removal from Detail (March 8, 2020):**
The CID Chief stated that he removed Complainant from his detail due to Complainant's failure to perform his basic duties as an ITU officer. The CID Chief explained that the Watch Commander specifically contacted Complainant to request assistance on a particular case and requested an expeditious response but Complainant failed to perform the task and also delegated the task to other members of the Tactical Terrorism Response Team. (ROI at 260)

## INVESTIGATION PROCESS

The investigator gave Complainant two weeks to submit his affidavit. (ROI at 198)

Complainant responded by requesting two weeks of administrative or sick leave to complete his affidavit. (ROI at 198)

On September 28, 2020, the day before Complainant's affidavit was originally due, the investigator provided Complainant an extension to complete his affidavit and Complainant was advised that he was approved for 16 hours of administrative leave for September 23-24, 2020. (ROI at 198)

Complainant did not submit an affidavit.

## AGENCY'S FINAL DECISION

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the Report of Investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ).

Complainant timely requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew his request.

The Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).

The decision found that Complainant did not establish a prima facie case because there was no evidence that other employees who were not members of his protected classes were treated differently.

The decision further found that even so, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions and Complainant did not submit any evidence of discriminatory animus.

The decision further found that Complainant did not establish that any of the alleged incidents of harassment were due to his protected classes.

The decision therefore concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

## APPEAL

Complainant appealed, contending that the investigation was inadequate and requesting that his case be referred to an AJ for additional investigation, as well as contending that the Agency's reasons are untrue.

In response, the Agency contends that Complainant was given adequate time to submit his affidavit but failed to do so and also failed to submit any evidence supporting his assertions of discriminatory animus.

- b. February 2019 to June 2019: the Branch Chief knew SCBPO-1 bullied and harassed Complainant and took no corrective action.
- c. April 17, 2019: SCBPO-1 verbally reprimanded Complainant for missing a morning training class.
- d. June 2019: SCBPO-1 showed a knife to Complainant and CBPO-2 and said he brings his knife collection to work in his backpack.
- e. June 3, 2019: SCBPO-1 reprimanded Complainant by email about his TECS access expiring.
- f. June 19, 2019: SCBPO-1 changed Complainant's schedule from 2:00 p.m. to 1:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. to celebrate the Chief's birthday and solicited $20 from him for the party.
- g. On or around August 16, 2019: SCBPO-1 and SCBPO-2 told coworkers that Complainant would be reassigned and leave the Intelligence Targeting Unit (ITU) effective September 1, 2019. He was not reassigned at that time.
- h. On or around August 16, 2019: SCBPO-1 and SCBPO-2 told Complainant his September 2019 leave request would not be approved. After he questioned them, the leave was approved.

**Claim 2:** Effective March 8, 2020, Complainant was removed from his detail in the ITU.

## Dismissed Claims (ROI at 150-57)
- Complainant learned on December 23, 2018 that he had not received a year-end monetary award.
- On April 21, 2019, SCBPO-1 charged Complainant with Leave Without Pay for untimely counselor contact. The number of hours is garbled in the record.
- Three claims alleging SCBPO-1 was unprofessional in speaking ill of three coworkers. These were dismissed for failure to state a claim because Complainant did not show he was aggrieved by comments about other employees.

## Agency Explanations (Sources as Stated in the Record)
- **Branch Chief (Memorandum of Counseling):** She stated she asked that the Memorandum be issued after Complainant was twice instructed not to put "E/O if not in vehicle" on a TECS record, because it creates a violation, and he continued not to comply. The citation appears to be ROI at 205, but it is split by a footnote in the record.
- **Intelligence Division Chief (CID Chief), Memorandum of Counseling:**
  - He explained that Complainant asked CBPOs to "exempt" travelers on primary who had illegal-activity links or ties, or whom he had targeted. He said this was essentially asking CBPOs to violate TECS policy.
  - He approved the Memorandum because Complainant did not follow instructions even after being asked twice. ROI at 259.
- **SCBPO-1, TECS access (ROI at 223-24):**
  - TECS sends automated periodic reminders starting 30 days before a user's recertification due date.
  - SCBPO-1 stated he received an automated email saying Complainant had lost access.
  - He then emailed Complainant to counsel him on the loss and remind him that he must maintain TECS access.
- **SCBPO-1, potluck and schedule (ROI at 224):**
  - The ITU traditionally organized optional "potlucks" or catering.
  - He stated he announced the potluck for 1:00 p.m. and told the 2:00 p.m. shift they could come in an hour early to participate.
  - Each employee was asked to donate $10 if they wished.
  - He stated that CBPO-1 gave him $20 to cover himself and Complainant after Complainant verbally said he wished to participate.
- **CID Chief, removal from detail (ROI at 260):**
  - He stated he removed Complainant for failure to perform basic ITU officer duties.
  - The Watch Commander contacted Complainant to request assistance on a particular case and asked for an expeditious response.
  - Complainant did not perform the task and delegated it to other members of the Tactical Terrorism Response Team.

## Procedural History
- The Agency gave Complainant the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of his right to a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). He timely requested a hearing and later withdrew the request.
- The Agency then issued a final decision under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).
- **Affidavit (ROI at 198):**
  - The investigator gave Complainant two weeks to submit an affidavit. He responded by asking for two weeks of administrative or sick leave to complete it.
  - On September 28, 2020, the day before the affidavit was originally due, the investigator gave an extension. Complainant was told he was approved for 16 hours of administrative leave for September 23-24, 2020. The record does not explain why these leave dates precede September 28.
  - Complainant did not submit an affidavit.

## Agency Final Decision: Criteria Applied and Findings
- Complainant did not establish a prima facie case, because there was no evidence that employees outside his protected classes were treated differently.
- Even so, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions, and Complainant submitted no evidence of discriminatory animus.
- Complainant did not establish that any alleged harassment incident was due to his protected classes.
- The Agency concluded he failed to prove discrimination as alleged.

## Appeal
- **Complainant:** He contends the investigation was inadequate and asks that the case be referred to an AJ for additional investigation. He also contends the Agency's reasons are untrue.
- **Agency:** It contends Complainant had adequate time to submit his affidavit but did not, and that he submitted no evidence supporting his assertions of discriminatory animus.

## Gaps in the Record
- The date of the Agency's final decision and the date of the appeal are not stated.
- The appellate decision-maker and the disposition of the appeal are not stated.
- The Agency's explanations for several sub-claims (1b, 1c, 1d, 1g, 1h) are not included in the excerpt.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Officer, GS-1895-12, at the Agency’s El Paso Port of Entry (POE), El Paso Field Office, Office of Field Operations in El Paso, Texas. On April 13, 2020, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency subjected her to a hostile work environment and discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female), disability (physical: cervical myelopathy, cervical fusion with limited neck movement) and age (56) when: 1. from September 8, 2019, to January of 2020, the Supervisory CBP Officer (Supervisor 1) assigned Complainant regular cashier duties in addition to issuing I-94s, despite the fact Complainant was on Light Duty; 2. in September of 2019, Supervisor 1 told the Program Manager that she did not want to work with Complainant in Passport Control Secondary because Complainant was on Light Duty and did not have a weapon. 3. on September 13, 2019, Supervisor 1 told Complainant that she did not want to work with her, and that Complainant was a liability due to her health issues; 4. from October 2019 to February 2020, on approximately 10 to 15 occasions, the Supervisor interrupted Complainant talking with other employees and asked them to stop talking; 5. on December 24, 2019, Supervisor 1 assigned Complainant passport control duties, despite the fact Complainant was on Light Duty. When Complainant explained she could help but could not perform regular duties for a full eight hours, the Supervisor replied "it is what it is;" 6. on December 24, 2019, in front of the public, Supervisor 1 yelled at Complainant to start issuing permits, stating Complainant does not want to do her job. Then, Supervisor 1 turned to the members of the public and advised them they could file a complaint against Complainant for not attending to them. 7. on January 1 and January 3, 2020, Supervisor 1 yelled at Complainant, accused her of doing a pat down and processing a case without a weapon while Complainant was on Light Duty, and accused her of abusing her light duty schedule; 8. on January 2, 2020, Supervisor 1 accused Complainant of making false statements in a memorandum; 9. on January 3, 2020, Supervisor 1 commented that Complainant did not want to work; 10. on January 3, 2020, after Supervisor 1 called the Chief regarding Complainant's schedule, Complainant's Light Duty shift was changed from the 10:00 p.m. -6:00 a.m. shift to the midnight-8 a.m. shift for two days before Complainant returned to full duty on her regular shift; 11. on January 6, 2020, Supervisor 1 yelled at Complainant over the phone, accusing her of working the wrong schedule and of not wanting to perform her duties; 12. on January 15 and 16, 2020, Supervisor 1 raised her tone, claimed Complainant did not want to do her job, threatened to give Complainant a verbal warning and reprimand for not taking over another officer's duties, and threatened to write Complainant up for insubordination and disobeying a direct order; 13. on January 16, 2020, when Complainant asked another Supervisory CBP Officer (Supervisor 2) to initial an assignment for her, he said "I'm not signing shit for you." Later, after Complainant refused to perform cashier duties, Supervisor 2 said he did not need a nonproductive worthless person there, and told her to go to the back of the office; 14. on January 31, 2020, Supervisor 1 approached Complainant in a threatening voice and demanded she perform cashier duties when three other officers were available. After Supervisor 1 called Supervisor 2, Supervisor 2 reassigned Complainant to detention log officer duties, raised his voice and demanded Complainant leave the work area and work from a different location. When Complainant did not, Supervisor 2 told Complainant to go home on administrative leave. Complainant did not go home; and 15. on February 6, 2020, Complainant received a Weingarten notice, was informed she was accused by Supervisor 1 and Supervisor 2 of not wanting to work, disobedience, neglecting duties and disobeying an order, and was asked to provide a written statement to the Chief. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The Agency found that Complainant failed to show that she was subjected to disparate treatment.

8. On January 2, 2020, Supervisor 1 accused Complainant of making false statements in a memorandum.

11. On January 6, 2020, Supervisor 1 yelled at Complainant over the phone, accusing her of working the wrong schedule and of not wanting to perform her duties.

13. On January 16, 2020, Supervisor 2 (another Supervisory CBP Officer) responded to Complainant's request to initial an assignment by saying "I'm not signing shit for you." **June 15, 2019:** The American Postal Workers Union, AFL-CIO, filed a Step 2 grievance against the Agency alleging that Complainant performing Clerk Craft duties in her Modified Assignment violated the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) because this crossed crafts. (ROI, Exhs. 4, 7, and Affidavit C, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates Nos. 180, 207, 146)

**June 21, 2019:** The HRM request for an updated medical note was repeated. (ROI, Affidavit A, at 16, Bates No. 21)

**July 2, 2019:** Complainant's doctor issued a letter stating: "Above mentioned patient physical requirements are lifting, pushing/pulling reaching above shoulder not to exceed 20lbs [sic.], standing and walking average time 20 minutes…."

**July 5, 2019:** Complainant came to work with the July 2, 2019 doctor's letter. From July 5, 2019 through July 31, 2019, she was not allowed to work. (ROI, Affidavit A, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 92)

**July 22, 2019:** HRM Manager wrote Complainant that the Agency was reviewing her Modified Assignment (Limited Duty) to determine if a revision was necessary after an arbitration award on limited duty "non-APWU Clerk craft employees performing clerk craft duty assignments." He informed her that management would perform a search for adequate, available work and, if found, she would be offered a revised Modified Assignment (Limited Duty) within her July 2, 2019 medical restrictions.

**July 25, 2019:** HRM Manager presented Complainant an Offer of Modified Assignment (Limited duty) effective August 1, 2019, to the position of Modified Handler (Modified Assignment – indefinite duration) at the James A. Farley Retail Local Operation Center. The duties were within the restrictions set forth in the July 2, 2019 doctor's letter. (ROI, Bates Nos. 25-26; Ex. 8, at 2, Bates No. 199)

**August 1, 2019:** Complainant returned to work.

**After July 31, 2019:** Complainant submitted a revised doctor's note. (ROI, Affidavit C, at four, ¶ 15, Bates No. 147)

## Key Statements

**Manager of Customer Services (S2):** 
- Stated the request for an updated medical note was made so the Agency could draft a new Offer of Modified Assignment for Complainant that was within her current medical restrictions and did not cross crafts. (ROI, Affidavit C, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 146)
- According to S2, HRM found the July 2, 2019 updated doctor's letter to be inadequate because the limitations were unclear, and he asked Complainant to submit another updated doctor's letter. (ROI, Affidavit C, at four, ¶ 15, Bates No. 147)
- S2 told Complainant not to return to work until she submitted an updated doctor's note describing her medical restrictions. (ROI, Affidavit A, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 92)

**Supervisor of Customer Services (S1):**
- Echoed that the request for an updated medical note was made so the Agency could draft a new Offer of Modified Assignment that was within Complainant's current medical restrictions and did not cross crafts. (ROI, Affidavit B, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 138)
- Attested that S2 told him HRM found the updated doctor's letter to be inadequate. (ROI, Affidavit C, at four, ¶ 15, Bates No. 147)

**HRM Manager:**
- Stated that S2 decided not to allow Complainant to work.
- Stated he was not aware why Complainant was not allowed to work in her limited duty assignment between July 5, 2019 and July 31, 2019.
- Learned of S2's decision after it was made.

**Complainant:**
- Does not contest that she performed Clerk Craft duties.
- Refused to submit a doctor's note with her current medical restrictions, believing it was unnecessary. (ROI, Affidavit A, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 92)
- Expected that when she brought in the updated note, she would be allowed to work.
- Erroneously alleged this period started on July 4, 2019, which was a paid holiday for her.

## Final Agency Decision (FAD)

The Agency found no discrimination.

**Criteria Applied:**
- Whether Complainant was an individual with a disability
- Whether Complainant was qualified to perform the essential functions of her Mail Handler (unmodified) job with or without reasonable accommodation
- Whether Complainant submitted the medical documentation management requested in order to offer her a new modified assignment within her medical limitations
- Whether Complainant proved discrimination under the theory of disparate treatment

**Decision-Maker:** The Agency (in the FAD)

**Responses Considered:**
- The Agency assumed, without finding, that Complainant was an individual with a disability.
- The Agency found she was not qualified because she was unable to perform the essential functions of her Mail Handler (unmodified) job with or without reasonable accommodation.
- The Agency reasoned that Complainant did not submit the medical documentation management requested in order to offer her a new modified assignment within her medical limitations.
- The Agency concluded Complainant did not prove discrimination under disparate treatment, noting that Complainant did not identify any comparative employees who were treated differently.

## Appeal

Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant later withdrew the request, the AJ ordered the Agency to issue a FAD. Complainant subsequently appealed the FAD. In reply, the Agency argued that the FAD should be affirmed.

On June 15, 2019, the American Postal Workers Union, AFL-CIO, filed a Step 2 grievance against the Agency alleging that Complainant performing Clerk Craft duties in her Modified Assignment violated the collective bargaining agreement (CBA) between the union and the Agency because this crossed crafts (i.e. someone outside the Clerk Craft performing Clerk Craft duties). Report of Investigation (ROI), Exhs. 4 (Step 2 grievance), 7 (Union request for a list of Complainant’s Modified Assignment duties), and Affidavit C, at 3, ¶ 15 (by the Manager of Customer Services, Complainant’s second line supervisor “S2”), Bates Nos. 180, 207, 146. Complainant does not contest that she performed Clerk Craft duties. On June 11, 2019, the Agency Health & Resource Management (HRM) informed Complainant that her most recent medical note on file was dated January 18, 2011, and it asked her to submit an updated note from her doctor with her medical restrictions. The request was repeated on June 21, 2019. ROI, at Affidavit A, at 16, Bates No. 21. S2 separately stated this request was made so the Agency could draft a new Offer of Modified Assignment for Complainant that was within her current medical restrictions and did not cross crafts. ROI, Affidavit C, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 146. The Supervisor of Customer Services, Complainant’s first line supervisor “S1” echoed this. Affidavit B, at 3, ¶ 15, Bates No. 138. However, Complainant refused to submit a doctor’s note with her current medical restrictions, believing it was unnecessary. At some point, S2 told Complainant not to return to work until she submitted an updated doctor’s note describing her medical restrictions. Affidavit A, at 3, ¶ 15, at Bates No. 92 (Complainant’s affidavit). Complainant expected that when she brought in the updated note, she would be allowed to work. On July 5, 2019, Complainant came to work with a July 2, 2019 doctor’s letter which read: … Above mentioned patient physical requirements are lifting, pushing/pulling reaching above shoulder not to exceed 20lbs [sic.], standing and walking average time 20 minutes…. According to S2, HRM found the updated doctor’s letter to be inadequate because the limitations were unclear. S2 stated that he asked Complainant to submit another updated doctor’s letter. Without reference to HRM, S1 attested that S2 told him the above. Complainant submitted a revised doctor’s note after July 31, 2019. ROI, Affidavit C, at four, ¶ 15 as continued from prior page, Bates No. 147. She returned to work on August 1, 2019. Complainant erroneously alleged this period started on July 4, 2019, which was a paid holiday for her. The HRM Manager stated it was S2 who decided not allow Complainant to work. According to HRM Manager, he learned this after S2 made the decision and he was not aware why Complainant was not allowed to work in her limited duty assignment between July 5, 2019 and July 31, 2019. On July 22, 2019, the HRM Manager wrote Complainant that the Agency was reviewing her Modified Assignment (Limited Duty) to determine if a revision was necessary after an arbitration award on limited duty “non-APWU Clerk craft employees performing clerk craft duty assignments.” He informed Complainant that management would perform a search for adequate, available work and, if found, she would be offered a revised Modified Assignment (Limited Duty) within her July 2, 2019 medical restrictions. Days later, in a letter dated July 25, 2019, the HRM Manager presented Complainant an Offer of Modified Assignment (Limited duty) effective August 1, 2019, to the position of Modified Handler (Modified Assignment – indefinite duration) at the James A. Farley Retail Local Operation Center. ROI, Bates Nos. 25 -26. The duties differed from her prior assignment, and the letter noted these duties were within the restrictions set forth in her “treating doctor [letter] dated July 2, 2019.” The list of Complainant’s restrictions in the Offer are identical to those listed in her July 2, 2019 doctor’s letter. ROI, Ex. 8, at 2, Bates No. 199. Following the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). But, even presuming she was otherwise qualified, the Agency reasoned that Complainant did not submit the medical documentation management requested in order to offer her a new modified assignment within her medical limitations. Additionally, the Agency concluded Complainant did not prove discrimination under the theory of disparate treatment. It found, for example, that Complainant did not identify any comparative employees who were treated differently. The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant argues that she was discriminated against. 3 In reply, the Agency argues that the FAD should be affirmed. Complainant raises allegations on appeal which are not part of her EEO complaint presently before us. Consequently, we shall not consider such claims in the instant decision.
