items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a probationary Credentials Assistant, GS-0303-07, at the Agency’s Naval Medical Center in Portsmouth, Virginia. On November 8, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (African-American) when she was terminated from her probationary position on August 2, 2018. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. The AJ held a hearing and subsequently issued a decision in favor of the Agency. The AJ first determined that Complainant’s theory of discrimination based on direct evidence was unreliable and found that neither Complainant nor her supporting witness were credible. At the hearing, Complainant testified that her second-level supervisor (S2), Department Head, GS- 0301-12, “made the decision to terminate her after learning that her ‘significant other’ was [W]hite.” Complainant testified that S2 became aware of Complainant’s relationship with a White man in May 2018, and that her relationship with S2 changed afterward. She also testified that her first-level supervisor (S1), Professional Affairs Coordinator (Assistant Department Head), GS-0301-11, “had warned [Complainant] not to let [S2] know she was dating a [W]hite man.” To corroborate her theory that S2 discriminated against her based on her race, Complainant presented a key witness, a coworker (CW), Program Analyst, GS-0303-07, who “testified that [S2] openly stated that [S2’s] husband was extremely biased against interracial relationships, and that she was surprised Complainant was dating a [W]hite man. [CW] claims she heard [S2] make other race-related remarks.” Both Complainant and CW testified that S1 had warned them about S2’s prejudice. 2 The AJ found this testimony lacked credibility “due to the glaring omission of any theory about Complainant’s interracial relationship in her complaint, EEO counseling records, or her affidavit [during the investigation].” The AJ reasoned that “[t]his type of evidence, if credible, would not have come up for the first time some three years after her termination.” During EEO counseling and in her affidavit, Complainant explained that she believed her termination stemmed from events that occurred during a work conference in Leesburg, Virginia, where S2 allegedly engaged in inappropriate behavior, and Complainant believed that S2 “did not trust [her] to not share what happened.” Complainant also had indicated that her termination was related to the fact that S2 thought Complainant had filed a grievance against her, though it had been another employee. The AJ noted that these prior theories Complainant posited before the hearing about why S2 terminated her “have no apparent connection to her race.” When cross-examined by Agency counsel during the hearing about the fact that she had not previously raised the theory of S2’s prejudice against interracial couples, Complainant provided no explanation for why she had not included it. Similarly, the AJ found that any reference to S2’s prejudice against interracial relationships was “conspicuously missing from [CW’s] affidavit” submitted during the investigation. CW’s affidavit referenced the events at the training in Leesburg and that she believed “Complainant was discriminated against because she was an African-American with more experience than management.” CW also stated in her affidavit that S1 had made racially inappropriate remarks but nowhere mentioned anything about Complainant’s partner being White or S2’s opposition to it. S1 testified during the hearing and denied making any comments about S2 being racist. The AJ found that the Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for Complainant’s termination. The reason, according to the Notice of Termination letter, was Complainant’s failure to “follow the privileging/credentialing process when [she] misrepresented to [her] leadership that a provider had specifically requested privileges when in fact [Complainant] made the request. According to the provider, [Complainant was] the one who tried to convince him to apply for privileges he did not previously hold.” This incident relates to a credentialing/privileges application submitted by the provider that Complainant helped process. In the application, the provider selected the incorrect privileges, which he had selected based on Complainant’s mistaken belief about the proper protocol for credentialing contract providers. Complainant’s guidance to the provider, which she acknowledged at the time was inaccurate, delayed the provider’s application and prevented him from receiving the proper credentials needed to practice within the Agency until the day his then-current privileges were set to expire. The provider then contacted Complainant’s supervisors “to express frustration with the delay in his application . . . [because Complainant] had provided him with incorrect guidance.” When her supervisors asked about the incident, Complainant explained to S1 that, before the provider’s discussion with Complainant, she had received an application from him within which he had improperly requested the incorrect privileges that he did not previously hold, and that her mistaken guidance was based on this prior application. After S2 obtained a written statement from the provider, S2 concluded that Complainant had misrepresented what happened, which provided part of the basis for Complainant’s termination. 3 The provider was a witness at the hearing, and the AJ found him credible when he testified that “he and Complainant discussed the [privileges] application before he submitted it” and that he submitted his application based on her instructions. The AJ found Complainant “not credible in her testimony that she never spoke to [the provider] prior to him submitting the [first] application.” The AJ therefore concluded that “Complainant has failed to prove pretext because there is no evidence that” the similarly situated employee named by Complainant “was involved in a similar episode, or that she was dishonest with her managers.” The AJ found Complainant’s testimony “simply unreliable” and that her “credibility is doubly important in this case because her lack of candor was part of why she was terminated.” The AJ therefore found that the Agency had not discriminated against Complainant as alleged. Part of Complainant’s Notice of Termination also included that Complainant “failed to initiate the renewal privileging/credentialing process within 90 days as required.” The AJ found, however, that it was untrue Complainant failed to do this, and that a similarly situated employee had several renewals nearing expiration with less than 90 days remaining but was not terminated. The AJ found that “[i]f this were the only reason for Complainant’s termination, she would be able to demonstrate pretext. But it was not.” When the Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ’s decision, the AJ’s decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged became the Agency’s final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). 4 The instant appeal followed.

- S2 made the decision to terminate her after learning that her "significant other" was White
- S2 became aware of Complainant's interracial relationship in May 2018
- Her relationship with S2 changed after May 2018
- S1 had warned Complainant not to let S2 know she was dating a White man

**Supporting Witness Testimony:**
Complainant presented a coworker (CW), Program Analyst, GS-0303-07, who testified that:
- S2 openly stated that S2's husband was extremely biased against interracial relationships
- S2 expressed surprise that Complainant was dating a White man
- S2 made other race-related remarks
- Both Complainant and CW testified that S1 had warned them about S2's prejudice

**AJ Credibility Findings:**
The AJ determined that:
- Complainant's theory of discrimination based on direct evidence was unreliable
- Neither Complainant nor her supporting witness (CW) were credible
- The testimony lacked credibility "due to the glaring omission of any theory about Complainant's interracial relationship in her complaint, EEO counseling records, or her affidavit [during the investigation]"
- The AJ reasoned that "[t]his type of evidence, if credible, would not have come up for the first time some three years after her termination"

**Prior Theories Advanced by Complainant:**

- She believed her termination stemmed from events that occurred during a work conference in Leesburg, Virginia, where S2 allegedly engaged in inappropriate behavior
- Complainant believed that S2 "did not trust [her] to not share what happened"
- Her termination was related to the fact that S2 thought Complainant had filed a grievance against her, though it had been another employee

The AJ noted that these prior theories "have no apparent connection to her race."

**Witness Affidavit Inconsistencies:**
- CW's affidavit submitted during the investigation referenced events at the training in Leesburg and stated that "Complainant was discriminated against because she was an African-American with more experience than management"
- CW's affidavit stated that S1 had made racially inappropriate remarks but made no mention of Complainant's partner being White or S2's opposition to it
- The reference to S2's prejudice against interracial relationships was "conspicuously missing from [CW's] affidavit"

**First-Level Supervisor's Testimony:**
S1 testified during the hearing and denied making any comments about S2 being racist.

**Agency's Stated Legitimate, Nondiscriminatory Reason for Termination:**
According to the Notice of Termination letter, Complainant was terminated for failure to "follow the privileging/credentialing process when [she] misrepresented to [her] leadership that a provider had specifically requested privileges when in fact [Complainant] made the request."

**Factual Basis for Stated Reason:**
- A provider's credentialing/privileges application was involved
- The provider selected incorrect privileges based on Complainant's mistaken belief about proper protocol for credentialing contract providers
- Complainant's inaccurate guidance delayed the provider's application and prevented him from receiving proper credentials until the day his then-current privileges were set to expire
- The provider contacted Complainant's supervisors to express frustration with the delay, stating that Complainant had provided incorrect guidance
- When supervisors asked about the incident, Complainant explained to S1 that she had received a prior application from the provider in which he had improperly requested incorrect privileges, and her mistaken guidance was based on that prior application
- S2 obtained a written statement from the provider, concluded that Complainant had misrepresented what happened, and this provided part of the basis for her termination

**Provider Witness Testimony:**
The provider testified at the hearing and the AJ found him credible when he testified that:
- He and Complainant discussed the privileges application before he submitted it
- He submitted his application based on her instructions

**AJ Credibility Finding Regarding Complainant:**
The AJ found Complainant "not credible in her testimony that she never spoke to [the provider] prior to him submitting the [first] application."

**Pretext Analysis:**
The AJ concluded that "Complainant has failed to prove pretext because there is no evidence that" a similarly situated employee named by Complainant "was involved in a similar episode, or that she was dishonest with her managers." The AJ found that Complainant's "credibility is doubly important in this case because her lack of candor was part of why she was terminated."

**Secondary Reason for Termination:**
The Notice of Termination also included that Complainant "failed to initiate the renewal privileging/credentialing process within 90 days as required."

The AJ found this claim to be untrue and noted that a similarly situated employee had several renewals nearing expiration with less than 90 days remaining but was not terminated. The AJ found that "[i]f this were the only reason for Complainant's termination, she would be able to demonstrate pretext. But it was not."

**Overall AJ Conclusion:**
The AJ found that the Agency had not discriminated against Complainant as alleged.

**Final Agency Action:**
When the Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ's decision, the AJ's decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged became the Agency's final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i).

**Appeal:**
The instant appeal followed the AJ's decision.

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

**Parties and Employment Information:**
- Complainant: Probationary Credentials Assistant, GS-0303-07, Naval Medical Center, Portsmouth, Virginia
- First-level Supervisor (S1): Professional Affairs Coordinator (Assistant Department Head), GS-0301-11
- Second-level Supervisor (S2): Department Head, GS-0301-12

**Complaint Filing:**
- Date of Termination: August 2, 2018
- Date EEO Complaint Filed: November 8, 2018
- Basis of Complaint: Discrimination based on race (African-American)

**Investigation and Hearing:**
- An Agency investigation was conducted, and Complainant was provided a copy of the investigation report with notice of her right to request an EEOC Administrative Judge hearing
- Complainant requested a hearing
- An EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) held a hearing and issued a decision in favor of the Agency

**Complainant's Theory of Discrimination:**
At the hearing, Complainant testified that:
- S2 made the decision to terminate her after learning that her "significant other" was White
- S2 became aware of Complainant's interracial relationship in May 2018
- Her relationship with S2 changed after May 2018
- S1 had warned Complainant not to let S2 know she was dating a White man

**Supporting Witness Testimony:**
Complainant presented a coworker (CW), Program Analyst, GS-0303-07, who testified that:
- S2 openly stated that S2's husband was extremely biased against interracial relationships
- S2 expressed surprise that Complainant was dating a White man
- S2 made other race-related remarks
- Both Complainant and CW testified that S1 had warned them about S2's prejudice

**AJ Credibility Findings:**
The AJ determined that:
- Complainant's theory of discrimination based on direct evidence was unreliable
- Neither Complainant nor her supporting witness (CW) were credible
- The testimony lacked credibility "due to the glaring omission of any theory about Complainant's interracial relationship in her complaint, EEO counseling records, or her affidavit [during the investigation]"
- The AJ reasoned that "[t]his type of evidence, if credible, would not have come up for the first time some three years after her termination"

**Prior Theories Advanced by Complainant:**
During EEO counseling and in her affidavit, Complainant had explained that:
- She believed her termination stemmed from events that occurred during a work conference in Leesburg, Virginia, where S2 allegedly engaged in inappropriate behavior
- Complainant believed that S2 "did not trust [her] to not share what happened"
- Her termination was related to the fact that S2 thought Complainant had filed a grievance against her, though it had been another employee

The AJ noted that these prior theories "have no apparent connection to her race."

**Witness Affidavit Inconsistencies:**
- CW's affidavit submitted during the investigation referenced events at the training in Leesburg and stated that "Complainant was discriminated against because she was an African-American with more experience than management"
- CW's affidavit stated that S1 had made racially inappropriate remarks but made no mention of Complainant's partner being White or S2's opposition to it
- The reference to S2's prejudice against interracial relationships was "conspicuously missing from [CW's] affidavit"

**First-Level Supervisor's Testimony:**
S1 testified during the hearing and denied making any comments about S2 being racist.

**Agency's Stated Legitimate, Nondiscriminatory Reason for Termination:**
According to the Notice of Termination letter, Complainant was terminated for failure to "follow the privileging/credentialing process when [she] misrepresented to [her] leadership that a provider had specifically requested privileges when in fact [Complainant] made the request."

**Factual Basis for Stated Reason:**
- A provider's credentialing/privileges application was involved
- The provider selected incorrect privileges based on Complainant's mistaken belief about proper protocol for credentialing contract providers
- Complainant's inaccurate guidance delayed the provider's application and prevented him from receiving proper credentials until the day his then-current privileges were set to expire
- The provider contacted Complainant's supervisors to express frustration with the delay, stating that Complainant had provided incorrect guidance
- When supervisors asked about the incident, Complainant explained to S1 that she had received a prior application from the provider in which he had improperly requested incorrect privileges, and her mistaken guidance was based on that prior application
- S2 obtained a written statement from the provider, concluded that Complainant had misrepresented what happened, and this provided part of the basis for her termination

**Provider Witness Testimony:**
The provider testified at the hearing and the AJ found him credible when he testified that:
- He and Complainant discussed the privileges application before he submitted it
- He submitted his application based on her instructions

**AJ Credibility Finding Regarding Complainant:**
The AJ found Complainant "not credible in her testimony that she never spoke to [the provider] prior to him submitting the [first] application."

**Pretext Analysis:**
The AJ concluded that "Complainant has failed to prove pretext because there is no evidence that" a similarly situated employee named by Complainant "was involved in a similar episode, or that she was dishonest with her managers." The AJ found that Complainant's "credibility is doubly important in this case because her lack of candor was part of why she was terminated."

**Secondary Reason for Termination:**
The Notice of Termination also included that Complainant "failed to initiate the renewal privileging/credentialing process within 180 days as required."

The AJ found this claim to be untrue and noted that a similarly situated employee had several renewals nearing expiration with less than 90 days remaining but was not terminated. The AJ found that "[i]f this were the only reason for Complainant's termination, she would be able to demonstrate pretext. But it was not."

**Overall AJ Conclusion:**
The AJ found that the Agency had not discriminated against Complainant as alleged.

**Final Agency Action:**
When the Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ's decision, the AJ's decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged became the Agency's final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i).

**Appeal:**
The instant appeal followed the AJ's decision.

It mentioned the Leesburg events and CW's belief that "Complainant was discriminated against because she was an African-American with more experience than management." It also said S1 made racially inappropriate remarks. It did not mention Complainant's partner being White or S2's opposition.

- The provider testified at the hearing, and the AJ found him credible. He said he and Complainant discussed the application before he submitted it and that he submitted it based on her instructions.
- The AJ found Complainant "not credible" in testifying that she never spoke to the provider before he submitted the first application. The AJ found her testimony "simply unreliable" and said her "credibility is doubly important in this case because her lack of candor was part of why she was terminated."
- The AJ concluded that Complainant failed to prove pretext because there was no evidence the similarly situated employee she named "was involved in a similar episode, or that she was dishonest with her managers."

The AJ also found that a similarly situated employee had several renewals nearing expiration with under 90 days remaining and was not terminated. The AJ stated: "If this were the only reason for Complainant's termination, she would be able to demonstrate pretext. But it was not."

- The Notice of Termination stated that Complainant failed to "follow the privileging/credentialing process when [she] misrepresented to [her] leadership that a provider had specifically requested privileges when in fact [Complainant] made the request."
- The provider said Complainant tried to convince him to apply for privileges he did not previously hold.
- The provider's application listed incorrect privileges, based on Complainant's mistaken belief about the protocol for credentialing contract providers. Complainant acknowledged at the time that her guidance was inaccurate.
- The guidance delayed the application until the day his then-current privileges were to expire. The provider then contacted Complainant's supervisors to express frustration, saying she had given him incorrect guidance.
- Complainant told S1 that the provider had already submitted an application requesting privileges he did not hold and that her guidance was based on it.
- S2 obtained a written statement from the provider and concluded Complainant had misrepresented what happened. This was part of the basis for the termination.

**Pretext analysis**
- The provider testified at the hearing, and the AJ found him credible. He said he and Complainant discussed the application before he submitted it and that he submitted it based on her instructions.
- The AJ found Complainant "not credible" in testifying that she never spoke to the provider before he submitted the first application. The AJ found her testimony "simply unreliable" and said her "credibility is doubly important in this case because her lack of candor was part of why she was terminated."
- The AJ concluded that Complainant failed to prove pretext because there was no evidence the similarly situated employee she named "was involved in a similar episode, or that she was dishonest with her managers."
- The Notice of Termination also said Complainant "failed to initiate the renewal privileging/credentialing process within 90 days as required." The AJ found this untrue. The AJ also found that a similarly situated employee had several renewals nearing expiration with under 90 days remaining and was not terminated. The AJ stated: "If this were the only reason for Complainant's termination, she would be able to demonstrate pretext. But it was not."
- The AJ found the Agency had not discriminated against Complainant as alleged.

**Final action and appeal**
- The Agency did not issue a final order within forty days of receiving the AJ's decision. Under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i), the AJ's decision therefore became the Agency's final action.
- Complainant then filed the instant appeal.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Travel Specialist, GS-6, at the Agency’s Office of Infectious Disease (OID), National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD and TB Prevention (NCHHSTP) in Atlanta, Georgia. Report of Investigation (ROI), at 49. 2 The Supervisor Program Specialist, GS-12, (female, African American) was assigned as Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1). Complainant was also supervised by the Management Officer (male, Caucasian) and the Deputy Director (male). Page numbers refer to the Bates page numbers appearing at the bottom center of each page of the ROI. According to Complainant, on October 28, 2013, in a meeting, S1 told her to get out of the Agency because upper management did not like her, the Management Officer was out to get her, and that she needed to get out of the “god damn” Union because it was never going to allow her to go anywhere in her career. ROI at 127. S1 denied making the comments and denied that the meeting or incident ever took place. Also, according to Complainant, the Support Specialist asked why she was not attending the Christmas party and asked if she celebrated Christmas. Id. at 129-30. Complainant apparently replied that she is a Jehovah’s Witness and does not celebrate Christmas. Id. Complainant averred that the Support Specialist “looked at her as if she had a disease” and rolled her eyes. Id. The Support Specialist did not recall having any interaction with Complainant on the day in question and maintained that the incident did not occur as Complainant alleged. Complainant additionally averred that on January 9, 2014, she overheard a coworker (C1) make the comment to another coworker (C2) that she (Complainant) thinks “she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and that she (Complainant) "is bad news and not your friend." Id. at 131- 32. Complainant maintained that such comments were made about her multiple times in hallways and in the elevator. Id. But C1 maintained that she had no idea who Complainant was and that she did not make any such comment. C2 similarly averred that she did not recall the comment being made to her by C1. Complainant further attested that the Deputy Director sexually harassed her on multiple occasions, which continued to the present. Complainant stated that the Deputy Director would stare at her chest, and he also put his hand on her left leg and “rolled his hand down” during two separate staff meetings. Id. at 133-35. Complainant said that she simply “scooted over” when the Deputy Director first put his hand on her leg. Id. She said that when this occurred a second time, she left in the middle of the meeting. Id. Complainant added that she told the Deputy Director to stop because the touching of her leg during the meeting was making her feel uncomfortable. Id. Complainant averred that the Deputy Director would also often come into her cubicle and put his hands on her shoulders, as if he were massaging her. Id. Complainant further stated that the Deputy Director would lean over her while showing her something on her computer, invading her personal space. Id. Complainant stated that the Deputy Director also asked her to lunch and/or dinner, but she rebuffed his advances. Id. Complainant attested that the Deputy Director punished her for rebuffing him by assigning her extra duties, refusing her requests for training, assigning her duties outside of her position description, and yelling and cursing at her in his office regarding the processing of employees travel preparations. Id. at 53. Complainant also attested that the Deputy Director would often call her into his office and “vent in a loud, angry voice while throwing things such as pens and pencils across the room.” Id. at 154. Complainant explained that she discussed the Deputy Director’s behavior with several of her coworkers. Complainant further explained that she reported the Deputy Director’s behavior just a few weeks after it first occurred to the Director, who simply shook his head in disbelief. Id. at 134. Complainant maintained that nothing was done to resolve the situation, and so the harassment continued. Id. Complainant stated that she further reported the Deputy Director’s harassment to S1, the Management Officer, and a Consultant with the Agency. Id. According to Complainant, these management officials ignored her complaints about the Deputy Director’s harassment towards her. Id. Nevertheless, both S1 and the Management Officer denied that Complainant ever reported the Deputy Director’s behavior to them, and so they were unaware of the Deputy Director’s alleged harassment. However, several of Complainant’s coworkers averred that Complainant had confided in them that the Deputy Director had been subjecting her to sexual harassment. The Senior Budget Analyst specifically attested that Complainant would come into her office, almost on a weekly basis, to vent about the Deputy Director violating her personal space and making her feel uncomfortable by asking her out and making inappropriate comments. Id. at 208. The Senior Budget Analyst said that she had witnessed the Deputy Director throw tantrums and yell as if Complainant was his “soundboard” on a few occasions. Id. The Senior Budget Analyst further averred that Complainant visited her office on several occasions crying over the Deputy Director’s behavior towards her. Id. The Team Lead similarly attested that Complainant also came to him on occasions to talk about the Deputy Director’s inappropriate behavior and that the Deputy Director had touched her inappropriately during a meeting. Id. at 205. The Team Lead averred that Complainant explained to him that she had scheduled a meeting with the Management Officer to discuss the Deputy Director’s conduct, and that Complainant later discussed the Management Officer’s lack of concern for addressing the alleged harassment. Id. The Team Lead added that he told Complainant that it seemed as if nothing would come as a result of her meeting with the Management Officer. Id. The Resource Management Team Lead also explained that she was frequently a “comforting ear” for Complainant, and that Complainant expressed her extreme discomfort with the Deputy Director’s behavior. Id. at 223. The Resource Management Team Lead stated that she had seen the Deputy Director in Complainant’s office many times, but she had not witnessed anything more than what she perceived to be an encroachment of Complainant’s personal space. Id. She mentioned she felt this to be unusual, but she had never directly witnessed the Deputy Director touch or address Complainant inappropriately. Id. The Public Health Advisor Supervisor likewise maintained that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had touched her leg and asked her out to dinner. Id. at 199. The Public Health Advisor attested that the Deputy Director had harassed her in the past as well, but she did not complain because she would have been the first women to have come forward. Id. The Public Health Advisor said that she was afraid to come forward because the Deputy Director was highly regarded within the Agency. Id. Another Team Lead, and two more employees, similarly stated that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had been harassing her. Complainant claimed, moreover, that S1 improperly scored her with the unsatisfactory rating of 2. for her mid-year performance review and placed her on a Performance Assistance Plan (PAP). Id. at 157-58. Complainant believed that S1’s review of her performance was especially improper because S1 would reportedly make comments to her, such as “Stop trying to act Black,” “Are you sure you’re not Black?” and “Don’t worry, we all know you’re Black.” Id. at 139. In the PAP issued to Complainant dated May 4, 2014, S1 noted that Complainant had failed to respond to customers concerning their travel tickets in a timely manner and failed to edit documentation to ensure the accuracy and completeness of travel reports, among other things. Id. at 335-40. Complainant was then subsequently placed on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) by S1 on September 22, 2014. Id. at 341-44. Therein, S1 noted that Complainant was rated, “Achieved Unsatisfactory Results" for her Customer Service rating. Id. S1 specifically noted that Complainant did not document and resolve complaints without assistance from her peers. Id. S1 further wrote that Complainant did not complete tasks in a timely manner and did not keep her customers up to date on their travel. Id. S1 also wrote, in the PIP, that Complainant received more than three customer complaints and a complaint from the Senior Federal Agency Travel Administrator (FATA). Id. S1 noted, for example, that the Senior FATA asked Complainant to correct a travel voucher for an employee, but Complainant required constant assistance from her peers to complete this task. Id. On October 16, 2014, Complainant received a Counseling Memorandum from S1. Id. at 345- 346. In the Memorandum, S1 noted that when she presented Complainant with the PIP on September 25, 2014, Complainant spoke in a loud and rude tone during the entire meeting. Id. S1 wrote that Complainant engaged in verbal abuse during the meeting, was not able to control her temper, and said she was being retaliated against, among other things. Id. S1 additionally noted that Complainant complained that she (S1) had been allowing her peers to call her a “wigger,” which meant “white [N-word].” Id. The Support Services Specialist observed, however, that Complainant was under extreme distress due to S1’s behavior towards Complainant. Id. at 202. The Support Services Specialist explained that one day she was in the copy room and Complainant came in shaking and she thought she would have to call an ambulance for Complainant. Id. According to the Support Services Specialist, Complainant proceeded to discuss the harassment she was experiencing from S1 and how often it was occurring. Id. Complainant additionally stated that on December 12, 2014, she was informed that was going to be transferred to another team away from S1’s supervision, so she could get a new start. Id. at 146-47. Complainant maintained that the transfer was good for her, as she noticed a more positive working environment. Id. Nevertheless, Complainant subsequently received her end-of- the year performance evaluation with the unsatisfactory rating of 2. from S1. Id. at 148-49. On April 8, 2014, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to harassment on the bases of race (Caucasian), national origin (German, Persian), sex (female), religion (Jehovah’s Witness, Jewish), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when: 1. On October 28, 2013, S1 told her to get out of the Agency because management do not like her, the Management Officer is out to get her, and she needs to get out of the god damn union because if she does not she is never going to go anywhere in her career. 2. On December 12, 2013, the Business Services Support Specialist approached her and berated her for not attending the office Christmas party. 3. On January 9, 2014, she overheard a coworker comment to another coworker about her that she "thinks she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and that she (Complainant) "is bad news and not your friend." 4. She has been subjected to sexual harassment by the Deputy Director from 2006 and continuing when he made unwanted advances toward her. The Deputy Director punished her for rebuffing him by assigning her extra duties, refusing her requests for training, assigning her duties which are outside of her position description, and yelling and cursing at her in his office regarding the processing of employees travel preparations. 5. On January 13, 2014, S1 told her to get the hell out of my office when she tried to explain to S1 that she had not been trained on the proper procedures for processing travel, among other things. 6. On July 28, 2014, she was given an unsatisfactory mid-year performance review with a rating of 2.06. 7. On May 5, 2014, she was placed on a Performance Assistance Plan (PAP). 8. On September 22, 2014, she was placed on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP). 9. On October 16, 2014, she was issued a Counseling Memorandum. 10. On December 12, 2014, she was advised that her supervisor would change from S1 to another supervisor on another team. 11. On January 29, 2015, she received a 2. on her end of year performance evaluation Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). In accordance with Complainant's request, the Agency issued a final decision (FAD) pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The Agency specifically found that Complainant did not establish that her allegations occurred as she alleged with regard to claims 1-3, and 5. The Agency determined, moreover, that Complainant’s allegations were not severe or pervasive enough to establish a hostile work environment. The Agency also found that Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to sexual harassment with regard to claim 4. But the Agency noted that no witnesses specifically observed the sexual harassment even though Complainant asserted that the events occurred in the workplace. The Agency further noted that while some witnesses described the Deputy Director as becoming angry and even throwing things, there was insufficient evidence to show that the Deputy Director sexually harassed Complainant. The Agency further found that management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions regarding claims 6-11, and that Complainant did not establish that its reasons were pretextual based on her protected classes. The Agency determined that Complainant did not show that it was motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes, and therefore Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to disparate treatment as alleged.

**Claim 4: Sexual Harassment by Deputy Director (2006 to Present)**

*Corroborating Witness Statements:*

The Senior Budget Analyst said she had witnessed the Deputy Director throw tantrums and yell as if Complainant was his "soundboard" on a few occasions. - **Resource Management Team Lead:** Explained that she was frequently a "comforting ear" for Complainant, and that Complainant expressed her extreme discomfort with the Deputy Director's behavior. She mentioned she felt this to be unusual, but she had never directly witnessed the Deputy Director touch or address Complainant inappropriately. (ROI, p. 223)

- **Public Health Advisor Supervisor:** Maintained that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had touched her leg and asked her out to dinner. The Public Health Advisor attested that the Deputy Director had harassed her in the past as well, but she did not complain because she would have been the first woman to have come forward. The Public Health Advisor said she was afraid to come forward because the Deputy Director was highly regarded within the Agency. (ROI, p. 199)

- **Additional Witnesses:** Another Team Lead and two more employees similarly stated that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had been harassing her.

---

**Claim 5: January 13, 2014 - Alleged Statement by S1**

*Complainant's Account:* S1 told her to "get the hell out of my office" when she tried to explain to S1 that she had not been trained on the proper procedures for processing travel.

---

**Claims Regarding Comments by S1 About Race:**

*Complainant's Account:* Complainant believed that S1's performance review was improper because S1 would reportedly make comments to her, such as "Stop trying to act Black," "Are you sure you're not Black?" and "Don't worry, we all know you're Black." (ROI, p. 139)

*Support Services Specialist's Observation:* The Support Services Specialist observed that Complainant was under extreme distress due to S1's behavior towards Complainant. The Support Services Specialist explained that one day she was in the copy room and Complainant came in shaking and she thought she would have to call an ambulance for Complainant. According to the Support Services Specialist, Complainant proceeded to discuss the harassment she was experiencing from S1 and how often it was occurring. (ROI, p. 202)

---

**Claim 6-11: Performance Reviews and Disciplinary Actions**

**Claim 6: July 28, 2014 - Mid-Year Performance Review**
Complainant claimed she was given an unsatisfactory mid-year performance review with a rating of 2.

**Claim 7: May 5, 2014 (issued May 4, 2014) - Performance Assistance Plan (PAP)**
Complainant was placed on a PAP by S1. (ROI, pp. 335-40) In the PAP, S1 noted that Complainant had failed to respond to customers concerning their travel tickets in a timely manner and failed to edit documentation to ensure the accuracy and completeness of travel reports, among other things.

**Claim 8: September 22, 2014 - Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)**
Complainant was placed on a PIP by S1. (ROI, pp. 341-44) In the PIP, S1 noted:
- Complainant was rated "Achieved Unsatisfactory Results" for her Customer Service rating
- Complainant did not document and resolve complaints without assistance from her peers
- Complainant did not complete tasks in a timely manner and did not keep her customers up to date on their travel
- Complainant received more than three customer complaints and a complaint from the Senior Federal Agency Travel Administrator (FATA)
- Example noted: The Senior FATA asked Complainant to correct a travel voucher for an employee, but Complainant required constant assistance from her peers to complete this task

**Claim 9: October 16, 2014 - Counseling Memorandum**
Complainant received a Counseling Memorandum from S1. (ROI, pp. 345-346) In the Memorandum, S1 noted that when she presented Complainant with the PIP on September 25, 2014, Complainant spoke in a loud and rude tone during the entire meeting. S1 wrote that Complainant engaged in verbal abuse during the meeting, was not able to control her temper, and said she was being retaliated against, among other things. S1 additionally noted that Complainant complained that she (S1) had been allowing her peers to call her a "wigger," which meant "white [N-word]."

**Claim 10: December 12, 2014 - Transfer of Supervision**
Complainant was informed that she was going to be transferred to another team away from S1's supervision so she could get a new start. (ROI, pp. 146-47) Complainant maintained that the transfer was good for her, as she noticed a more positive working environment.

**Claim 11: January 29, 2015 - End-of-Year Performance Evaluation**
Complainant subsequently received her end-of-year performance evaluation with the unsatisfactory rating of 2 from S1. (ROI, pp. 148-49)

---

## FORMAL COMPLAINT

**Filing Date:** April 8, 2014

**Alleged Bases:** Race (Caucasian), national origin (German, Persian), sex (female), religion (Jehovah's Witness, Jewish), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity

**Eleven Specific Allegations Listed:**
1. October 28, 2013 - S1's statements about getting out of the Agency
2. December 12, 2013 - Business Services Support Specialist berating her for not attending Christmas party
3. January 9, 2014 - Coworker comments about her appearance and character
4. Sexual harassment by Deputy Director from 2006 to present with retaliatory actions
5. January 13, 2014 - S1 telling her to get out of office
6. July 28, 2014 - Unsatisfactory mid-year performance review (rating 2.06)
7. May 5, 2014 - Placement on Performance Assistance Plan
8. September 22, 2014 - Placement on Performance Improvement Plan
9. October 16, 2014 - Issuance of Counseling Memorandum
10. December 12, 2014 - Change of supervisor
11. January 29, 2015 - End-of-year performance evaluation (rating 2)

---

## FINAL AGENCY DECISION (FAD)

**Standard Applied:** Pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b)

**Decision:** The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

**Specific Findings:**

*Claims 1-3 and 5:*
- Complainant did not establish that her allegations occurred as she alleged
- No evidence corroborated Complainant's version of events with regard to her allegations that S1 subjected her to a hostile work environment
- Complainant's allegations were not severe or pervasive enough to establish a hostile work environment

*Claim 4 (Sexual Harassment by Deputy Director):*
- Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to sexual harassment
- The Agency noted that several witnesses reported that Complainant was so devastated by the Deputy Director's harassing behavior that she frequently vented about his conduct and was seen crying and shaking in their offices
- However, no witnesses specifically observed the sexual harassment even though Complainant asserted that the events occurred in the workplace
- While some witnesses described the Deputy Director as becoming angry and even throwing things, there was insufficient evidence to show that the Deputy Director sexually harassed Complainant

*Claims 6-11 (Performance Reviews and Disciplinary Actions):*
- Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions
- Complainant did not establish that the reasons were pretextual based on her protected classes
- Complainant did not show that actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes
- Therefore, Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to disparate treatment as alleged

# CASE FILE SUMMARY

**Position and Workplace:**
Complainant worked as a Travel Specialist, GS-6, at the Agency's Office of Infectious Disease (OID), National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD and TB Prevention (NCHHSTP) in Atlanta, Georgia. (ROI, p. 49)

**Supervisory Structure:**
- First-level supervisor (S1): Supervisor Program Specialist, GS-12 (female, African American)
- Additional supervisors: Management Officer (male, Caucasian) and Deputy Director (male)

---

## ALLEGATIONS AND EVIDENCE

**Claim 1: October 28, 2013 - Alleged Statements by S1**

*Complainant's Account:* S1 told her to get out of the Agency because upper management did not like her, the Management Officer was out to get her, and she needed to get out of the "god damn" Union because it would never allow her to advance her career. (ROI, p. 127)

*S1's Response:* S1 denied making the comments and denied that the meeting or incident ever took place.

---

**Claim 2: December 12, 2013 - Alleged Interaction with Support Specialist**

*Complainant's Account:* The Support Specialist asked why she was not attending the Christmas party and asked if she celebrated Christmas. Complainant replied that she is a Jehovah's Witness and does not celebrate Christmas. The Support Specialist "looked at her as if she had a disease" and rolled her eyes. (ROI, pp. 129-30)

*Support Specialist's Response:* The Support Specialist did not recall having any interaction with Complainant on the day in question and maintained that the incident did not occur as Complainant alleged.

---

**Claim 3: January 9, 2014 - Alleged Comments by Coworkers**

*Complainant's Account:* Complainant overheard coworker C1 make comments to coworker C2 that she (Complainant) thinks "she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and that she "is bad news and not your friend." Complainant maintained that such comments were made about her multiple times in hallways and in the elevator. (ROI, pp. 131-32)

*C1's Response:* C1 maintained that she had no idea who Complainant was and that she did not make any such comment.

*C2's Response:* C2 averred that she did not recall the comment being made to her by C1.

---

**Claim 4: Sexual Harassment by Deputy Director (2006 to Present)**

*Complainant's Account:* The Deputy Director sexually harassed her on multiple occasions. Complainant stated that:
- The Deputy Director would stare at her chest (ROI, pp. 133-35)
- He put his hand on her left leg and "rolled his hand down" during two separate staff meetings (ROI, pp. 133-35)
- During the first incident, Complainant "scooted over"
- During the second incident, she left in the middle of the meeting
- Complainant told the Deputy Director to stop because the touching was not making her feel uncomfortable (ROI, p. 133-35)
- The Deputy Director would often come into her cubicle and put his hands on her shoulders, as if massaging her (ROI, p. 133-35)
- He would lean over her while showing her something on her computer, invading her personal space (ROI, p. 133-35)
- He asked her to lunch and/or dinner, which she rebuffed (ROI, p. 133-35)

*Alleged Retaliatory Actions:* Complainant attested that the Deputy Director punished her for rebuffing him by:
- Assigning her extra duties
- Refusing her requests for training
- Assigning her duties outside of her position description
- Yelling and cursing at her in his office regarding the processing of employees' travel preparations (ROI, p. 53)
- Calling her into his office and "venting in a loud, angry voice while throwing things such as pens and pencils across the room" (ROI, p. 154)

*Reports Made:* Complainant reported the Deputy Director's behavior:
- To the Director "just a few weeks after it first occurred," who "simply shook his head in disbelief" (ROI, p. 134)
- To S1, the Management Officer, and a Consultant with the Agency
- Complainant maintained that nothing was done and the harassment continued (ROI, p. 134)

*S1 and Management Officer's Response:* Both S1 and the Management Officer denied that Complainant ever reported the Deputy Director's behavior to them, and stated they were unaware of the alleged harassment.

*Corroborating Witness Statements:*

- **Senior Budget Analyst:** Attested that Complainant would come into her office almost on a weekly basis to vent about the Deputy Director violating her personal space and making her feel uncomfortable by asking her out and making inappropriate comments. The Senior Budget Analyst said she had witnessed the Deputy Director throw tantrums and yell as if Complainant was his "soundboard" on a few occasions. The Senior Budget Analyst further averred that Complainant visited her office on several occasions crying over the Deputy Director's behavior towards her. (ROI, p. 208)

- **Team Lead:** Attested that Complainant came to him on occasions to talk about the Deputy Director's inappropriate behavior and that the Deputy Director had touched her inappropriately during a meeting. The Team Lead averred that Complainant explained she had scheduled a meeting with the Management Officer to discuss the Deputy Director's conduct, and that Complainant later discussed the Management Officer's lack of concern for addressing the alleged harassment. The Team Lead added that he told Complainant that it seemed as if nothing would come as a result of her meeting with the Management Officer. (ROI, p. 205)

- **Resource Management Team Lead:** Explained that she was frequently a "comforting ear" for Complainant, and that Complainant expressed her extreme discomfort with the Deputy Director's behavior. The Resource Management Team Lead stated that she had seen the Deputy Director in Complainant's office many times, but she had not witnessed anything more than what she perceived to be an encroachment of Complainant's personal space. She mentioned she felt this to be unusual, but she had never directly witnessed the Deputy Director touch or address Complainant inappropriately. (ROI, p. 223)

- **Public Health Advisor Supervisor:** Maintained that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had touched her leg and asked her out to dinner. The Public Health Advisor attested that the Deputy Director had harassed her in the past as well, but she did not complain because she would have been the first woman to have come forward. The Public Health Advisor said she was afraid to come forward because the Deputy Director was highly regarded within the Agency. (ROI, p. 199)

- **Additional Witnesses:** Another Team Lead and two more employees similarly stated that Complainant had mentioned that the Deputy Director had been harassing her.

---

**Claim 5: January 13, 2014 - Alleged Statement by S1**

*Complainant's Account:* S1 told her to "get the hell out of my office" when she tried to explain to S1 that she had not been trained on the proper procedures for processing travel.

---

**Claims Regarding Comments by S1 About Race:**

*Complainant's Account:* Complainant believed that S1's performance review was improper because S1 would reportedly make comments to her, such as "Stop trying to act Black," "Are you sure you're not Black?" and "Don't worry, we all know you're Black." (ROI, p. 139)

*Support Services Specialist's Observation:* The Support Services Specialist observed that Complainant was under extreme distress due to S1's behavior towards Complainant. The Support Services Specialist explained that one day she was in the copy room and Complainant came in shaking and she thought she would have to call an ambulance for Complainant. According to the Support Services Specialist, Complainant proceeded to discuss the harassment she was experiencing from S1 and how often it was occurring. (ROI, p. 202)

---

**Claim 6-11: Performance Reviews and Disciplinary Actions**

**Claim 6: July 28, 2014 - Mid-Year Performance Review**
Complainant claimed she was given an unsatisfactory mid-year performance review with a rating of 2.

**Claim 7: May 5, 2014 (issued May 4, 2014) - Performance Assistance Plan (PAP)**
Complainant was placed on a PAP by S1. (ROI, pp. 335-40) In the PAP, S1 noted that Complainant had failed to respond to customers concerning their travel tickets in a timely manner and failed to edit documentation to ensure the accuracy and completeness of travel reports, among other things.

**Claim 8: September 22, 2014 - Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)**
Complainant was placed on a PIP by S1. (ROI, pp. 341-44) In the PIP, S1 noted:
- Complainant was rated "Achieved Unsatisfactory Results" for her Customer Service rating
- Complainant did not document and resolve complaints without assistance from her peers
- Complainant did not complete tasks in a timely manner and did not keep her customers up to date on their travel
- Complainant received more than three customer complaints and a complaint from the Senior Federal Agency Travel Administrator (FATA)
- Example noted: The Senior FATA asked Complainant to correct a travel voucher for an employee, but Complainant required constant assistance from her peers to complete this task

**Claim 9: October 16, 2014 - Counseling Memorandum**
Complainant received a Counseling Memorandum from S1. (ROI, pp. 345-346) In the Memorandum, S1 noted that when she presented Complainant with the PIP on September 25, 2014, Complainant spoke in a loud and rude tone during the entire meeting. S1 wrote that Complainant engaged in verbal abuse during the meeting, was not able to control her temper, and said she was being retaliated against, among other things. S1 additionally noted that Complainant complained that she (S1) had been allowing her peers to call her a "wigger," which meant "white [N-word]."

**Claim 10: December 12, 2014 - Transfer of Supervision**
Complainant was informed that she was going to be transferred to another team away from S1's supervision so she could get a new start. (ROI, pp. 146-47) Complainant maintained that the transfer was good for her, as she noticed a more positive working environment.

**Claim 11: January 29, 2015 - End-of-Year Performance Evaluation**
Complainant subsequently received her end-of-year performance evaluation with the unsatisfactory rating of 2 from S1. (ROI, pp. 148-49)

---

## FORMAL COMPLAINT

**Filing Date:** April 8, 2014

**Alleged Bases:** Race (Caucasian), national origin (German, Persian), sex (female), religion (Jehovah's Witness, Jewish), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity

**Eleven Specific Allegations Listed:**
1. October 28, 2013 - S1's statements about getting out of the Agency
2. December 12, 2013 - Business Services Support Specialist berating her for not attending Christmas party
3. January 9, 2014 - Coworker comments about her appearance and character
4. Sexual harassment by Deputy Director from 2006 to present with retaliatory actions
5. January 13, 2014 - S1 telling her to get out of office
6. July 28, 2014 - Unsatisfactory mid-year performance review (rating 2.06)
7. May 5, 2014 - Placement on Performance Assistance Plan
8. September 22, 2014 - Placement on Performance Improvement Plan
9. October 16, 2014 - Issuance of Counseling Memorandum
10. December 12, 2014 - Change of supervisor
11. January 29, 2015 - End-of-year performance evaluation (rating 2)

---

## FINAL AGENCY DECISION (FAD)

**Standard Applied:** Pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b)

**Decision:** The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

**Specific Findings:**

*Claims 1-3 and 5:*
- Complainant did not establish that her allegations occurred as she alleged
- No evidence corroborated Complainant's version of events with regard to her allegations that S1 subjected her to a hostile work environment
- Complainant's allegations were not severe or pervasive enough to establish a hostile work environment

*Claim 4 (Sexual Harassment by Deputy Director):*
- Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to sexual harassment
- The Agency noted that several witnesses reported that Complainant was so devastated by the Deputy Director's harassing behavior that she frequently vented about his conduct and was seen crying and shaking in their offices
- However, no witnesses specifically observed the sexual harassment even though Complainant asserted that the events occurred in the workplace
- While some witnesses described the Deputy Director as becoming angry and even throwing things, there was insufficient evidence to show that the Deputy Director sexually harassed Complainant

*Claims 6-11 (Performance Reviews and Disciplinary Actions):*
- Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions
- Complainant did not establish that the reasons were pretextual based on her protected classes
- Complainant did not show that actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes
- Therefore, Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to disparate treatment as alleged

# Case File Summary

## 1. Background
- Complainant was a Travel Specialist, GS-6, at the Agency's Office of Infectious Disease (OID), National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD and TB Prevention (NCHHSTP), in Atlanta, Georgia. (ROI at 49.)
- Her supervisors were:
  - S1, the Supervisor Program Specialist, GS-12 (female, African American), her first-level supervisor.
  - The Management Officer (male, Caucasian).
  - The Deputy Director (male).
- ROI page numbers are the Bates numbers at the bottom center of each page.

## 2. Complainant's Statements and Responses

**Claim 1: October 28, 2013 meeting with S1** (ROI at 127)
- *Complainant:* S1 told her to get out of the Agency because upper management did not like her and the Management Officer was out to get her. S1 also said she needed to get out of the "god damn" Union because it would never let her advance.
- *S1:* Denied making the comments and denied that the meeting or incident took place.

**Claim 2: Christmas party** (ROI at 129-30)
- *Complainant:* The Support Specialist asked why she was not attending the Christmas party and whether she celebrated Christmas. Complainant apparently replied that she is a Jehovah's Witness and does not celebrate Christmas. She said the Support Specialist "looked at her as if she had a disease" and rolled her eyes.
- *Support Specialist:* Did not recall any interaction with Complainant that day and maintained the incident did not occur as alleged.

**Claim 3: January 9, 2014 overheard comment** (ROI at 131-32)
- *Complainant:* She overheard coworker C1 tell coworker C2 that Complainant thinks "she is cute because she is built like a Black girl" and that she "is bad news and not your friend." Complainant said similar comments were made multiple times in hallways and the elevator.
- *C1:* Had no idea who Complainant was and did not make the comment.
- *C2:* Did not recall C1 making the comment to her.

**Claim 4: Alleged sexual harassment by the Deputy Director**
- *Complainant's account:*
  - The harassment occurred on multiple occasions and continued to the present. (ROI at 133-35.)
  - He stared at her chest.
  - He put his hand on her left leg and "rolled his hand down" during two separate staff meetings. She "scooted over" the first time and left the meeting the second time. She told him to stop because it made her uncomfortable. (Id.)
  - He often came into her cubicle and put his hands on her shoulders as if massaging her. (Id.)
  - He leaned over her at her computer, invading her personal space. (Id.)
  - He asked her to lunch and/or dinner, and she rebuffed him. (Id.)
  - He punished her for rebuffing him by assigning extra duties, refusing training requests, assigning duties outside her position description, and yelling and cursing at her in his office about processing employees' travel preparations. (Id. at 53.)
  - He often called her into his office and would "vent in a loud, angry voice while throwing things such as pens and pencils across the room." (Id. at 154.)
- *Reports by Complainant:*
  - She discussed his behavior with several coworkers.
  - She reported it to the Director a few weeks after it first occurred. The Director "simply shook his head in disbelief," and nothing was done. (Id. at 134.)
  - She also reported it to S1, the Management Officer, and a Consultant, who she said ignored her complaints. (Id.)
- *S1 and the Management Officer:* Both denied that Complainant ever reported the Deputy Director's behavior to them and said they were unaware of the alleged harassment.
- *Coworker statements:*
  - **Senior Budget Analyst** (ROI at 208): Complainant came to her office almost weekly to vent about the Deputy Director violating her personal space, asking her out, and making inappropriate comments. She had seen him throw tantrums and yell as if Complainant were his "soundboard" on a few occasions. Complainant visited her office several times crying over his behavior.
  - **Team Lead** (ROI at 205): Complainant talked to him about the Deputy Director's inappropriate behavior and said he had touched her inappropriately during a meeting. She told him she scheduled a meeting with the Management Officer and later spoke of the Management Officer's lack of concern. He told her it seemed nothing would come of that meeting.
  - **Resource Management Team Lead** (ROI at 223): She was frequently a "comforting ear" for Complainant, who expressed extreme discomfort with the Deputy Director. She had seen him in Complainant's office many times and perceived an encroachment of personal space, which she felt was unusual. She never directly witnessed him touch or address Complainant inappropriately.
  - **Public Health Advisor Supervisor** (ROI at 199): Complainant mentioned that he touched her leg and asked her to dinner.
  - **Public Health Advisor** (ROI at 199): He had harassed her in the past as well. She did not complain because she would have been the first woman to come forward and was afraid, since he was highly regarded within the Agency.
  - **Another Team Lead and two more employees:** Each stated that Complainant had mentioned the Deputy Director was harassing her.

**Claims 6-8 and 11: Performance rating, PAP, PIP, and year-end rating**
- *Complainant:* S1 improperly gave her an unsatisfactory mid-year rating of 2. and placed her on a Performance Assistance Plan (PAP). (ROI at 157-58.) She considered the review especially improper because S1 reportedly made comments such as "Stop trying to act Black," "Are you sure you're not Black?" and "Don't worry, we all know you're Black." (Id. at 139.)
- *PAP dated May 4, 2014* (ROI at 335-40): S1 noted that Complainant failed to respond to customers about travel tickets in a timely manner and failed to edit documentation for accuracy and completeness of travel reports, among other things.
- *PIP, September 22, 2014* (ROI at 341-44): S1 recorded that Complainant was rated "Achieved Unsatisfactory Results" for Customer Service. S1 noted that Complainant:
  - did not document and resolve complaints without peer assistance;
  - did not complete tasks timely or keep customers updated on their travel;
  - received more than three customer complaints and a complaint from the Senior Federal Agency Travel Administrator (FATA).
  
  As an example, S1 noted that the Senior FATA asked Complainant to correct an employee's travel voucher and she needed constant peer assistance to do so.
- *End-of-year evaluation:* Complainant received an unsatisfactory rating of 2. from S1. (ROI at 148-49.)

**Claim 9: Counseling Memorandum, October 16, 2014** (ROI at 345-46)
- *S1's account in the Memorandum:*
  - When S1 presented the PIP on September 25, 2014, Complainant spoke in a loud and rude tone throughout the meeting, engaged in verbal abuse, could not control her temper, and said she was being retaliated against, among other things.
  - Complainant complained that S1 allowed peers to call her a "wigger," meaning "white [N-word]."
- *Support Services Specialist* (ROI at 202): Complainant was under extreme distress due to S1's behavior. Once, in the copy room, Complainant came in shaking, and the Specialist thought she would need to call an ambulance. Complainant then described the harassment she was experiencing from S1 and how often it occurred.

**Claim 10: Transfer, December 12, 2014** (ROI at 146-47)
- *Complainant:* On December 12, 2014, she was told she would be moved to another team away from S1's supervision so she could get a new start. She said the transfer was good for her and she noticed a more positive working environment.

## 3. Procedural History
- **April 8, 2014:** Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging discrimination and harassment based on:
  - race (Caucasian);
  - national origin (German, Persian);
  - sex (female);
  - religion (Jehovah's Witness, Jewish);
  - reprisal for prior protected EEO activity.
- **Accepted claims:**
  1. October 28, 2013: S1's statements about leaving the Agency and the union.
  2. December 12, 2013: the Business Services Support Specialist berated her for not attending the Christmas party.
  3. January 9, 2014: the overheard coworker comment.
  4. Sexual harassment by the Deputy Director from 2006, continuing, with the alleged punishments described above.
  5. January 13, 2014: S1 told her to "get the hell out of my office" when she said she had not been trained on proper travel processing procedures, among other things.
  6. July 28, 2014: unsatisfactory mid-year review, rating 2.06.
  7. May 5, 2014: placed on the PAP.
  8. September 22, 2014: placed on the PIP.
  9. October 16, 2014: Counseling Memorandum.
  10. December 12, 2014: told her supervisor would change from S1 to another supervisor on another team.
  11. January 29, 2015: received a 2. on her end-of-year evaluation.
- After the investigation, the Agency gave Complainant the ROI and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). At Complainant's request, the Agency issued a final decision (FAD) under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The record does not state the FAD's date.

## 4. Decision
**Decision-maker:** The Agency, through its final decision. The record names no individual.

**Outcome:** Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

**Findings and criteria applied:**
- **Claims 1-3 and 5:**
  - *Finding:* Complainant did not establish that the events occurred as alleged. There was no evidence corroborating her version of events on the allegation that S1 subjected her to a hostile work environment.
  - *Criterion:* The allegations were not severe or pervasive enough to establish a hostile work environment.
- **Claim 4 (sexual harassment):**
  - *Finding:* Complainant did not establish that she was sexually harassed.
  - *Evidence considered:*
    - Several witnesses reported that Complainant was devastated by the Deputy Director's behavior, frequently vented about it, and was seen crying and shaking in their offices.
    - No witness specifically observed the sexual harassment, although Complainant said the events occurred in the workplace.
    - Some witnesses described the Deputy Director becoming angry and even throwing things, but the evidence was insufficient to show he sexually harassed Complainant.
- **Claims 6-11 (disparate treatment):**
  - *Finding:* Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions, and Complainant did not show those reasons were pretextual based on her protected classes.
  - *Criterion:* She did not show the actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes, so she did not establish disparate treatment.

## 5. Discrepancies in the Record (for the investigator's attention)
- The PAP is dated May 4, 2014 (ROI at 335-40), but claim 7 lists the placement as May 5, 2014.
- The EEO complaint is stated as filed April 8, 2014, yet it lists events dated after that (July 2014 through January 29, 2015).
- The narrative gives no date for the Christmas party exchange. Claim 2 gives December 12, 2013.
- The record gives no citation for S1's alleged January 13, 2014 statement (claim 5), and no ROI citation for the Agency's findings.
- The mid-year rating is given as "2." in the narrative and "2.06" in claim 6.

(Id. at 139.)
- *PAP dated May 4, 2014* (ROI at 335-40): S1 noted that Complainant failed to respond to customers about travel tickets in a timely manner and failed to edit documentation for accuracy and completeness of travel reports, among other things.

  8. September 22, 2014: placed on the PIP.

  11. January 29, 2015: received a 2. on her end-of-year evaluation.
- After the investigation, the Agency gave Complainant the ROI and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). At Complainant's request, the Agency issued a final decision (FAD) under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The record does not state the FAD's date.

## 4. Decision
**Decision-maker:** The Agency, through its final decision. The record names no individual.

**Outcome:** Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

**Findings and criteria applied:**
- **Claims 1-3 and 5:**
  - *Finding:* Complainant did not establish that the events occurred as alleged. There was no evidence corroborating her version of events on the allegation that S1 subjected her to a hostile work environment.
  - *Criterion:* The allegations were not severe or pervasive enough to establish a hostile work environment.
- **Claim 4 (sexual harassment):**
  - *Finding:* Complainant did not establish that she was sexually harassed.
  - *Evidence considered:*
    - Several witnesses reported that Complainant was devastated by the Deputy Director's behavior, frequently vented about it, and was seen crying and shaking in their offices.
    - No witness specifically observed the sexual harassment, although Complainant said the events occurred in the workplace.
    - Some witnesses described the Deputy Director becoming angry and even throwing things, but the evidence was insufficient to show he sexually harassed Complainant.
- **Claims 6-11 (disparate treatment):**
  - *Finding:* Management articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions, and Complainant did not show those reasons were pretextual based on her protected classes.
  - *Criterion:* She did not show the actions were motivated by discriminatory animus based on her protected classes, so she did not establish disparate treatment.

## 5. Discrepancies in the Record (for the investigator's attention)
- The PAP is dated May 4, 2014 (ROI at 335-40), but claim 7 lists the placement as May 5, 2014.
- The EEO complaint is stated as filed April 8, 2014, yet it lists events dated after that (July 2014 through January 29, 2015).
- The narrative gives no date for the Christmas party exchange. Claim 2 gives December 12, 2013.
- The record gives no citation for S1's alleged January 13, 2014 statement (claim 5), and no ROI citation for the Agency's findings.
- The mid-year rating is given as "2." in the narrative and "2.06" in claim 6.

Complainant originally included a claim of reprisal for prior EEO activity in her complaint, but she withdrew the reprisal claim during a conference before the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). 1. On May 31, 2018, July 3, 2018, and July 16, 2018, Complainant’s first-level supervisor (S1), Force Development Flight Chief, GS-0301-13, claimed to have given a verbal counseling to Complainant; however, no documentation was generated in Complainant’s personnel file; 2. On October 18, 2018, Complainant was given a Letter of Reprimand by S1; 3. On February 12, 2019, March 14, 2019, March 21, 2019, April 2, 2019, and April 3, 2019, S1 accepted incorrect statements from Complainant’s subordinates; 4. On April 25, 2019, Complainant was given a Notice of Proposed Removal letter, signed by S1; 5. On or about June 28, 2019, Complainant was mailed a Decision to Remove letter dated June 28, 2019, signed by S1; and 6. On October 22, 2019, Complainant learned her Common Access Card (CAC) was still active, which would allow others to modify Complainant’s existing work even though Complainant is no longer with the Agency and had to surrender her CAC when removed from federal service. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. Over Complainant’s objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment in favor of the Agency. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. The AJ found that, taking the facts as presented in the report of investigation and viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, she failed to create a genuine issue of material fact to establish discrimination based on race, sex, color, or age. We note that although the AJ analyzed Claim 6 as part of Complainant’s complaint in the decision granting the Agency’s motion for summary judgment, Complainant does not list the claim in her brief on appeal and does not dispute the AJ’s finding of no discrimination with regard to Claim 6. We will therefore not address this claim further. As to the remaining claims, the AJ found that Complainant could not prove that she had been subjected to disparate treatment or discriminatory harassment. Assuming Complainant could establish a prima facie case of discrimination for Claims 4 and 5, the AJ found that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. The AJ determined that S1 decided to remove Complainant, as stated in the Notice of Proposed Removal letter, because of her “[f]ailure to meet suspenses [i.e., deadlines] in a timely manner,” “cancelling scheduled events without permission from leadership,” “not stagger[ing] schedules to meet the needs of [her] events and patrons,” “not reliev[ing] staff members for lunches or breaks,” not conducting “staff planning meetings for events,” staff accusations that Complainant “gossip[s] and release[s] privileged information about employees with other staff members,” “[s]taff members fear[ing] retaliation, bad feedbacks and appraisals if they speak up,” and “[l]ack of attention to detail with funds management.” Moreover, the AJ found that Complainant was unable to identify similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably than her. Complainant pointed to coworkers who were not disciplined for having a fight in front of patrons, but the AJ found that “Complainant was terminated for an entirely different set of circumstances and reasons” and that “both women [coworkers] hold a different type of position than Complainant,” so were therefore not adequately similar. In analyzing Complainant’s claims of a hostile work environment due to harassment, the AJ concluded that Complainant had not met her burden. Complainant’s harassment claims consisted of the following: S1’s indication in the Notice of Proposed Removal letter that she had given verbal counseling to Complainant on three separate occasions but had not documented it in Complainant’s personnel file 3; S1’s issuance of a Letter of Reprimand to Complainant for “leaving the library unattended to deal with a personal issue, thereby blocking [a summer] intern from the building,”; S1’s acceptance of allegedly inaccurate statements from Complainant’s White subordinates about Complainant’s conduct at work without further investigation; and Complainant’s proposed removal and ultimate termination from the Agency. First, the AJ found that Complainant could not link any of the harassment allegations to her protected bases. Regarding her alleged bases of sex and age, the AJ determined that “Complainant fails to offer any evidence tying her age or sex to any of the listed events other than her own conclusory statements.” As to race and color, the AJ found that Complainant’s statements “speculat[ing] that because Complainant is Black and her supervisor and subordinates are not, there was some kind of conspiracy to get her fired . . . does not, by itself, show racial animus.” The AJ also addressed an affidavit by one of Complainant’s coworkers who supported Complainant’s contention that the work environment was racially hostile. The AJ acknowledged that the coworker averred “that unnamed staff members stated they disliked being supervised by an African American” and that a subordinate coworker and S1 both “complained that Complainant was not experienced enough and that Complainant’s predecessor, who is Caucasian, did a better job.” However, the AJ found the coworker’s affidavit “very confusing,” and noted that “[h]e appears to have learned of these alleged instances second or third-hand, as opposed to witnessing them himself.” Because Complainant provided no other evidence showing these statements had occurred as the coworker alleged, the AJ determined that “the uncorroborated statement of [the coworker], without more, does not establish racial animus on the part of [S1] or Complainant’s subordinates.” In addition to the AJ’s conclusion that Complainant failed to show a nexus between the alleged incidents and her protected bases, the AJ found that “Complainant has failed to establish that she was subjected to severe and pervasive harassment in the form of unwelcome verbal or physical conduct sufficient to change her employment conditions into an abusive working environment.” An Agency employee, Chief Human Resources Officer, GS-0201-12, stated in her affidavit that verbal counseling is not required to be added to personnel files.
